name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Proposed Lincoln City Charter amendments must appear on Nov. 3 ballot, Supreme Court says
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that Lincoln voters will see at least three proposed city charter amendments on their ballot this fall In an unsigned, 20-page ruling, the high court decided 5-2 that Lincoln city officials must place the qualifying three proposals from the Good Government Lincoln campaign on the Nov. 3 ballot. […]
text:
Justices of the Nebraska Supreme Court (and when they were seated), front row from left: William Cassel (2012), Jeffrey Funke (2016, 2024 as chief justice) and Stephanie Stacy (2015). Back row, from left: Jason Bergevin (2025), Jonathan Papik (2018), John  Freudenberg (2018) and Derek Vaughn (2026). (Courtesy of the Nebraska Judicial Branch)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that Lincoln voters will see at least three proposed city charter amendments on their ballot this fall
In an unsigned, 20-page ruling, the high court decided 5-2 that Lincoln city officials must place the qualifying three proposals from the Good Government Lincoln campaign on the Nov. 3 ballot. City officials had contended that because they did not have time for at least two meetings prior to a Sept. 1 deadline, the measures would instead appear on the May 4, 2027, ballot.
“We grant the petition … commanding respondents (Lincoln city officials to submit the proposed charter amendments to a vote of the qualified electors at the next general election held on Nov. 3, 2026,” the majority opinion states.
The seven-member Lincoln City Council. Top row, from left, Sändra Washington, Justin P. Carlson, Tom Beckius and James Michael Bowers. Bottom row, from left, Tom Duden (vice chair), Brodey Weber (chair) and Bennie Shobe. (Photo courtesy of City of Lincoln)
The three petitions seek to limit Lincoln City Council members to two consecutive four-year terms, move the dates of city elections from odd to even years and let certain residents within a 3-mile buffer around Lincoln city limits vote in municipal elections, excluding bond votes.
But there could be more proposals on the Lincoln ballot, as the court unanimously left open the door for the Lincoln City Council to put forward alternatives for Lincoln voters to choose from, an option the Lincoln city attorney hinted remains on the table.
“Nothing in this opinion should be read to impair any constitutional right to submit ‘any alternative article or section’ under Neb. Const. Art. XI, Section 4,” the Supreme Court wrote.
‘Supreme Court has spoken’
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers filed the case Aug. 27, the same night he asked city officials to confirm whether they would place the measures on the November ballot. All three measures have enough valid signatures this time around — all three fell short in an initial batch of signatures submitted in mid-July, most of those flagged as possibly fraudulent.
The lawsuit was filed against all seven members of the Lincoln City Council and the city clerk.
Hilgers, who lives outside Lincoln in the 3-mile “extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction,” described Wednesday’s ruling as important not just for Lincoln residents “but for the rule of law in Nebraska.” He has acknowledged he is a supporter of the group’s efforts.
“The Lincoln voters did the hard work of gathering enough signatures to earn a spot on the November ballot. Unfortunately, Lincoln’s elected officials decided to play political games instead of obeying the Constitution,” Hilgers said in a statement.
‘Sad period in Nebraska history’: AG Hilgers speaks on ongoing petition fraud investigations

“I am grateful to the Supreme Court for protecting the right of the people of Lincoln to participate in their government at the ballot box this fall,” Hilgers continued. “City officials do not get to ignore the Constitution. My office will continue to stand up for the rights of Nebraskans whenever local governments try to sideline them.”
Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie and the seven-member Lincoln City Council had agreed that they needed to forward the qualifying measure to voters, but they disagreed on when. They interpreted the constitution’s “next general or special election” requirement as the city’s next general election, which is May 4, 2027.
The Supreme Court majority cited past precedent that a “general” election is used “interchangeably and synonymously” with “regular” election, so November is the right date.
Christie said Wednesday the “Supreme Court has spoken, and we will comply with their order.”
“We are disappointed that the review and approval timeline has been shortened due to alleged fraud in the Good Government ballot initiative process,” Yohance said in a statement.
A dissenting opinion
Justice Stephanie Stacy of Lincoln, writing in dissent, said the majority’s conclusion “is not supported by the constitutional text and is contrary to the Lincoln City Charter.”
“Although this court has construed similar language in statutes,  we have not, until today, construed the constitutional text,” Stacy wrote in her almost 10-page dissent.
Nebraska Supreme Court Justice Stephanie Stacy. Dec. 2, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
She said submitting a strictly local matter to Lincoln voters at the next statewide general election will require the Lincoln City Council to ignore provisions of its charter and violate established timeframes under state law in the Election Act, a concern Christie echoed Wednesday.
Said Stacy: “Because the city council has no clear legal duty under either Lincoln’s home rule charter or current Nebraska statute to submit the charter amendment petitions to city voters any sooner than May 2027, it should not be compelled to do so.”
Stacy added that she saw nothing that supported a need to expedite the matter or outlined any specific harm that would occur if the charter amendments instead went to voters in May 2027.
“But even assuming some harm could be shown from such a delay, I am not persuaded it would outweigh the consequences of granting the peremptory writ in this case, and the disorder and confusion it is likely to cause to election officials and electors,” Stacy wrote.
Court of Appeals Judge Michael W. Pirtle of Omaha joined Stacy’s dissent. He filled in for Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke, who did not participate in the case.
City opens door to ‘alternatives’
Christie said the city is concerned that “sacrificing steps in the public process undermines public understanding and confidence in the ballot process and does not allow for adequate time to educate the public on the impacts of the charter amendments.”
“Nevertheless, the city will move forward and will place the charter amendments and any alternatives on the November ballot,” Christie said.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers hosts a news conference in his office in the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
City Council Chair Brodey Weber said in an Aug. 31 affidavit to the Supreme Court that he and other members of the Lincoln City Council had “expressed an interest in considering or offering alternative amendments” to the proposals from Good Government Lincoln.
However, Weber said officials needed “adequate time to constructively engage in the legislative process” as a reason for the delay to next May.
Former state Sen. Tony Fulton, a sponsor of Good Government Lincoln, celebrated Wednesday’s. He said in a statement:
“We are thrilled that the voters of Lincoln will have the final say on term limits, increased voter participation in city elections, and that every citizen who is subject to Lincoln government is able to vote on the officials who are ultimately governing them.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Sens. Hoeven, Grassley see more to do for ranchers amid Trump plan to import beef
description: Republican Sens. John Hoeven of North Dakota and Chuck Grassley of Iowa say they want to help U.S. beef producers grow their herds while President Donald Trump plans to import 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef meant to lower prices for consumers. The two senators spoke with reporters after Grassley and his wife, Barbara, toured […]
text:
Republican U.S. Sens. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, left, and John Hoeven of North Dakota talk to reporters from the North Dakota Capitol on Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)Republican Sens. John Hoeven of North Dakota and Chuck Grassley of Iowa say they want to help U.S. beef producers grow their herds while President Donald Trump plans to import 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef meant to lower prices for consumers.
The two senators spoke with reporters after Grassley and his wife, Barbara, toured the North Dakota Capitol on Wednesday. The Grassleys had earlier toured the Minnesota Capitol, and were on their way next to the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library at Medora. 
Grassley said the president’s announcement last month might discourage investment needed to increase the U.S. cattle herd, which is at a 75-year low. However, improvements in feeding and genetics have led to more meat coming off of cattle – resulting in a record 28.4 billion pounds of beef produced in 2022. 
“All the money that it takes to restore the number of cattle we need to have a balance between production and consumer prices is going to have to come with increased numbers,” Grassley told reporters.
Hoeven said, “Fundamentally, we want to work with our ranchers to grow our herds” and also increase competition in the slaughter industry and address supply-chain issues.
Beef producers ‘disappointed’ by Trump tariff suspension

The senators also lauded other Trump administration and farm bill proposals to help the herd supply such as allowing more flexibility for the Conservation Reserve Program so more land can be grazed and cut for hay. Other policies support more competition for the “big four” meatpackers with local or small-scale processing or slaughter and labeling requirements for meat so consumers know if they are buying imported or U.S. beef.
About 60% of U.S. cattle were in drought areas as of Sept. 1, according to a U.S. Department of Agriculture report. In North Dakota, 82% of cattle were in drought areas, according to the same report.
North Dakota had 1.73 million head of cattle and calves as of Jan. 1, according to USDA. The U.S. had more than 86 million head at that time.
Ground beef has been at record average prices in the U.S. in recent months, as high as $7.14 a pound in June, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: LIV Golf declares bankruptcy owing Louisiana $1.2M for canceled event
description: Louisiana’s incentive package for LIV Golf included $2.2 million to upgrade a New Orleans golf course for the event and a $5 million “hosting fee” for LIV Golf.
text:
Brendan Steele of HyFlyers GC hits his shot during the final round of LIV Golf Adelaide at the Grange Golf Club in Adelaide, Australia. The state of Louisiana may not be able to fully recover $1.2 million from LIV Golf for a canceled New Orleans tournament after the organization filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. (Photo by Chris Trotman/LIV Golf)LIV Golf still owes the state of Louisiana $1.2 million after canceling a golf tournament that was supposed to take place in New Orleans in June. 

The state of Louisiana is listed as the 20th largest creditor in paperwork LIV Golf filed Tuesday as part of its request for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in a New Jersey federal court. Several pro golfers are among those owed the most money, but Louisiana is the only government entity listed among creditors with the largest unsecured claims. 

“LIV has formally acknowledged that they owe the state the money. The issue is now in the hands of the bankruptcy court,” Emma Wagner, a spokesperson for Louisiana Economic Development, wrote in a text message Wednesday. 

The state was expected to spend $7.2 million to bring LIV Golf to the Bayou Oaks at City Park golf course in late June. The event was indefinitely postponed in late April after news broke that LIV Golf’s Saudi Arabian backers were pulling their funding from the professional tour. 

Louisiana’s incentive package included $2.2 million in funding to upgrade the golf course for the event and a $5 million “hosting fee” for LIV Golf. 

The upgrades that were planned at the New Orleans course still moved forward, with improvements made at its driving range and to tee boxes for two holes, according to Jacob Peters, executive director of the Bayou District Foundation, which operates the golf course. 

The $1.2 million LIV Golf owes Louisiana represents the portion of the $5 million hosting fee the state had given to the tour before it called off the New Orleans tournament. The money was supposed to be refunded if the event never happened, according to the state’s arrangement with LIV Golf. 

The organization’s decision to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection makes the possibility of full repayment to its creditors far less certain, according to The New York Times. 
Gov. Jeff Landry unveiled initial plans for LIV Golf’s New Orleans tour stop in August 2025 with much fanfare. The announcement at City Park included a DJ, brass band, pyrotechnics and a pro wrestling-style hype man. 
Bubba Watson, a Pensacola, Florida, native who was one of the biggest stars on the LIV Golf tour was also on hand for the kickoff party with Landry last year. The bankruptcy court documents filed in New Jersey show LIV Golf now owes Watson at least $3.3 million. 

Louisiana’s decision to spend money on the LIV Golf tournament was controversial from the outset. At the time, the tour’s largest backer was Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, one of the richest sovereign wealth funds in the world with nearly $1 trillion in assets. Critics wondered why Louisiana needed to give $5 million to an organization with so many resources at the time. 
Saudi Prime Minister and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who oversees the fund, has been accused of human rights abuses. 

The $7.2 million incentive for LIV Golf came from Louisiana’s major events funds, which has also been used to lure the Super Bowl, Essence Festival and NCAA Men’s Final Four to the state.

name: VTDigger
title: Gov. Scott vetoed state regulations on data centers. One of his deputies just urged Congress to pass them.
description:
Gov. Scott vetoed state regulations on data centers. One of his deputies just urged Congress to pass them.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Gov. Scott vetoed state regulations on data centers. One of his deputies just urged Congress to pass them..
text:
Julie Moore, secretary of the Agency of Natural Resources, speaks about flooding in the state during a press conference in Berlin on Monday, Dec. 18, 2023. Photo by Natalie Williams/VTDigger

Vermont’s secretary of natural resources testified before a U.S. Congressional committee last week in support of a bill that would direct states to limit the costs consumers shoulder for the water used by data centers.
Julie Moore told lawmakers she supports “requiring owners and operators to help pay for the water infrastructure impacts they create,” as well as studying the potential impacts data centers could have on nearby water sources.
Her testimony in Washington, D.C. — a rarity for Vermont officials — came just months after her boss, Republican Gov. Phil Scott, vetoed a bipartisan bill in Vermont that would have created a new regulatory framework for large data centers in the state, including measures that are similar to those proposed in the federal legislation.
Two of the Vermont bill’s leading supporters said they were surprised to hear the secretary’s testimony given Scott has continued, as recently as last week, to say he does not think Vermont needs new state-level regulations aimed at data centers. 
Many of the facilities, which provide the computing power behind the boom in artificial intelligence technology, consume massive amounts of water for cooling and other purposes. In some cases, data centers built in recent years have faced backlash for discharging pollutants into local waterways. Vermont’s bill was wide-ranging and included far more than just water regulations — but Moore was nevertheless conveying to Congress some of its key goals, said Dan Fingas, the executive director of Vermont Conservation Voters. That’s one of the organizations that lobbied for the bill this year.
“I do think there’s a contradiction,” he said in an interview. “This testimony from Secretary Moore to Congress shows that they’ve already seen areas where Vermont is left unprotected — or, at least, needs more protection.”
Moore, in an interview, pushed back on that characterization. She said her testimony was unrelated to the reasons Scott rejected the bill, namely that he believes Vermont already has sufficient regulations in place to scrutinize a proposed large data center and that the bill went too far by subjecting the facilities to overly burdensome standards.
The Scott administration broadly supports the principle that ratepayers living near a data center should not have to pay higher costs to accommodate it, she said — but “that wasn’t at the crux of the governor’s veto.”
Her testimony comes as debate over how Vermont communities should prepare for the possible development of a data center has continued apace. In the absence of a state law, three cities and towns have passed regulations aimed at prohibiting data centers, at least temporarily, Seven Days reported Wednesday. In Vernon, one company has eyed the former Vermont Yankee site for a data center project, or something else, it has said.
Moore’s comments also come as data centers have become a major political issue nationally in the leadup to the midterm elections in November. Recent polling shows data centers, especially those used for artificial intelligence, are becoming increasingly unpopular with voters. Vermont Conservation Voters launched a public campaign last week called “Don’t Data Center Vermont,” to highlight what the organization says are the harmful impacts the facilities could have by using up large amounts of water, electricity and land, as well potentially causing pollution.
The bulk of Moore’s testimony, to a subcommittee of the U.S. House Committee on Commerce and Energy, focused on urging lawmakers to boost funding for a joint federal and state program that provides low-cost loans to public water systems to help them comply with the federal government’s drinking water safety standards. She was speaking on behalf of both the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources and a national association of the leaders of state and tribal environmental agencies.
But Moore also voiced support for the Water Cost Accountability Act, which would direct states to prevent public water systems from charging anyone other than the developers or operators of a data center for that facility’s water usage, or for the costs of expanding a system to accommodate a new data center. It would also require the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to study where data centers get their water. 
As of last week, the bill was in the initial stage of consideration in the House and a final version had yet to be formally introduced. 
The subcommittee’s chair, U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Al., said during the hearing that the draft legislation would balance business needs with protecting consumers.
Data centers “can have positive impacts on local communities. They are major drivers of investment, economic growth, job creation and the development of our nation’s digital infrastructure,” he said. “However, those benefits should not come at the expense of families and small businesses through higher water rates.”
Vermont’s bill, meanwhile, would have created new safeguards from the potential water quality impacts of large data centers and helped shield water ratepayers from the costs of operating those data centers, among other measures, Fingas said. 
The bill, H.727, would have required a data center that uses water for cooling to employ what’s known as a closed-loop system, which circulates a fixed volume of water rather than constantly drawing in fresh water. If a facility did not use a closed system, it would have to “minimize water use and not unreasonably burden a public water supply,” the bill said. 
The legislation also would have required data centers to submit quarterly reports to the state on their water usage and required an additional layer of review for facilities using more than 150,000 gallons of water a day for cooling or other purposes. 
The bill passed both the Vermont House and Senate with broad support. Scott’s veto caught many legislators by surprise; the House later came within just seven votes of overriding it. Advocates have already said they plan to push for a revised regulatory framework in the upcoming legislative session, which starts in January. 
Fingas, of Vermont Conservation Voters, said he was happy to hear Moore talk about the impacts of data centers to Congress, but “I wish she was doing that more in our state.”
Ben Edgerly Walsh, climate and energy program director at the Vermont Public Interest Research Group, which also lobbied for H.727, agreed, calling the regulations Moore testified in support of “common sense.”
Edgerly Walsh said in an interview that he doesn’t think a federal bill regulating data centers would amount to much, though, because he expects President Donald Trump would veto it.
Trump has voiced strong support for the industry, writing in a post on his Truth Social platform last month that “the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” 
As Edgerly Walsh sees it, “we’re not going to see meaningful federal protections. So, we have to look to what we can do as Vermonters,” he said.
Gov. Scott, for his part, reiterated his opposition to new statewide data center regulations during his weekly press conference last week. 
Scott said he was not opposed to cities and towns adopting their own policies but thought that, like the statewide bill, it would be unnecessary because there are few if any existing proposals to build such a facility in the state. 
“I think the likelihood of a data center in Vermont, anywhere, in the future, is slim to none,” he said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa farmers argue Hinson’s Save Our Bacon act would hurt small producers
description: ELKHART —  Some Iowa producers argued Wednesday that the federally proposed Save Our Bacon Act will harm farmers by taking away diversified markets and by sending a message to consumers that they are not entitled to a choice in what they eat.  The Save Our Bacon Act is a bill introduced by U.S. Rep. Ashley […]
text:
John Gilbert speaks at a farm in Elkhart, Iowa Sept. 9, 2026 in opposition to the Save Our Bacon Act. Behind him is Chris Petersen, left, John Norris, center, and Tony Thompson, right. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) ELKHART —  Some Iowa producers argued Wednesday that the federally proposed Save Our Bacon Act will harm farmers by taking away diversified markets and by sending a message to consumers that they are not entitled to a choice in what they eat. 
The Save Our Bacon Act is a bill introduced by U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for U.S. Senate, to block individual states from enforcing conditions on livestock products sold across state lines. 
The bill seeks to protect livestock producers from a “patchwork” of state laws, like California’s Proposition 12, that stipulates the growing conditions of certain livestock, including hogs.
While proponents of the bill argue it keeps other states from telling producers how to raise their animals, opponents of the bill say it protects the industrialized agriculture model and punishes farmers who have innovated their operations to sell into diversified markets. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Aaron Lehman, president of Iowa Farmers Union, spoke at a news conference Wednesday and said instead of the Save Our Bacon Act, lawmakers should be focusing on “real, structural” changes to agriculture that will help struggling farmers, like mandatory country of origin labeling, the enforcement of antitrust laws, support for local meat processing and to greater connections between producers and consumers.
“We know how to make meaningful changes to help Iowa livestock farmers,” Lehman said. “We just need the political will to demand that they be put in place. The Save Our Bacon Act won’t get it done.” 
Proposition 12 in California originally passed in 2018, but was not fully implemented until 2024, following a U.S. Supreme Court decision that upheld the state’s law that requires, among other things, that certain pork products sold in the state come from hogs that were given at least 24 square feet of usable floorspace.
A spokesperson for Hinson said Iowa farmers “overwhelmingly oppose” Proposition 12. 
“Ashley Hinson has listened to them and led the fight against anti-ag activists trying to tell Iowa farmers how to raise their livestock,” the spokesperson said in a statement. 
The Save Our Bacon Act was adopted in the House-passed farm bill but was not part of the Senate version, which is still in committee. 
Pork producers in the state, and nationally, have said the added costs of complying with Proposition 12 would negatively impact the next generation of hog producers, and they argue it makes pork products — including bacon — cost more at the grocery store.
 Opponents of Save Our Bacon, however, argue that producers don’t have to sell their proteins to California if they don’t want to comply with the state’s law. 
Tony Thompson, a farmer and candidate for the Iowa Senate, said the bill would prevent markets from rewarding farmers who “do something different.” 
He argued that while big producers are competitive by producing more product, faster and cheaper, smaller producers are competitive by being innovative with stewardship practices and quality standards. 
“Small family farms aren’t going to win a race against multinational, vertically integrated corporations on producing the cheapest pound of protein,” Thompson said. “Frankly, I don’t want them to, because when lowest cost becomes the only goal, everything else starts to look like a cost to be eliminated.” 
The Save Our Bacon Act has garnered support from Iowa Pork Producers Association, Iowa Farm Bureau Federation and other agricultural interest groups from around the country. Iowa Farm Bureau’s political action committee has also endorsed Hinson in the U.S. Senate race against Democrat Josh Turek who has said he opposes the Save Our Bacon Act.
John Gilbert, a Hardin County farmer who said dairy and hogs have been the “linchpins” in his operation, said the Save Our Bacon Act would “punish” producers who have invested in operational upgrades to be compliant with the California law. 
A spokesperson for the Hinson campaign argued the bill would give farmers and consumers a choice in producing or purchasing protein that met certain standards. Without the bill, they argued, farmers are forced to comply with the regulation. 
Gilbert said he was also concerned that the bill would “negate” other state laws, including some in Iowa, that work to protect the livestock industry from importing animals with diseases. 
A legislative analysis from Harvard Law School identified 13 Iowa laws that would be potentially impacted by the Save Our Bacon Act. 
Gilbert said the most “egregious and insulting” element of the Save Our Bacon Act is the message it sends to consumers.
“People like you and me, it’s telling people you don’t have a right … you’re not entitled to have a say in what you eat,” Gilbert said.  
Producers and lawmakers have been fighting on the issue — spurred by  Proposition 12 — for several years. Prior to the Save Our Bacon Act, lawmakers in Congress tried to pass the Ending Agricultural Trade Suppression Act, or EATS act, to similarly stop states from enacting such laws. 
Lehman said the topic is an issue in this election because “farmers are hurting” and the Save Our Bacon Act would “make problems for farmers even worse.”
“It is essential that we address corporate consolidation in agriculture,” Lehman said. “Farmers receive less than 15 cents out of every food dollar spent in our country. This is the reason that even when farmers struggle to make a living, consumers are still paying higher and higher prices at the grocery store.”

title: Help for Vermont Guard families is getting a home of its own
description:
The $6.6 million center will bring financial, legal and mental health services together at Camp Johnson.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Help for Vermont Guard families is getting a home of its own.
text:
Major General Hank Harder, adjutant general of the Vermont National Guard, speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony for the new Vermont Army National Guard Family Readiness Center at Camp Johnson in Colchester on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
COLCHESTER — A deployment can leave a military spouse managing the bills, child care and every problem at home alone. A new center at Camp Johnson is intended to ease some of that strain.
“We understand that the Vermont National Guard is a family, and that family is not just the men and women in uniform. It is the people back home, especially the children,” U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Wednesday.
Vermont National Guard officials and members of the state’s congressional delegation broke ground Wednesday on the Family Readiness and Support Center in Colchester. The federally funded center will consolidate services now scattered across Camp Johnson for service members, veterans and their families.
“What you do to help each other is so necessary,” U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., told the Guard members and families. “But for most of the country, including Vermont, it’s invisible. Life goes on.”
The center will offer legal assistance, financial counseling, retirement services and suicide-prevention support, according to Maj. Gen. Henry “Hank” Harder Jr., adjutant general of the Vermont National Guard.
Guard families can face a range of practical problems during a deployment, Vermont National Guard spokesperson Joseph Brooks said. A spouse may need financial counseling or help finding child care after the household’s primary earner leaves. In other cases, the person at home must learn to handle tasks, such as repairing a dishwasher, that the deployed family member would normally manage.
“This means that instead of trying to hunt around this post, we can send them to one place,” Brooks said.

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony for the new Vermont Army National Guard Family Readiness Center at Camp Johnson in Colchester on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Harder said the building also is meant to show families that their needs are central to the Guard’s mission.
“It’s about what we say to our families when they walk through the door: a modern, welcoming, purpose-built facility that tells them that they are a priority and not an afterthought, tucked into whatever space happens to be available,” Harder said.
Sanders secured $4.6 million for the project through the fiscal 2022 congressional spending process. Planning later stalled when pandemic-era inflation drove construction costs above that appropriation, Harder said.
Welch later worked with Sanders to secure an additional $2 million. Federal funding will cover the center’s construction, according to Guard officials.
Wednesday’s ceremony came days after members of the Vermont Air National Guard returned from an eight-month deployment to the Caribbean and Middle East.
“This has been a very long deployment,” Welch said. “It’s also in very harsh conditions. Our soldiers out there did not have the resupply that is normally available and should be available.”
Welch said families also shoulder the consequences of deployment, often without their neighbors understanding what they are experiencing. The isolation can be especially acute in rural Vermont, where many Guard families live far from Camp Johnson and one another.
“They’re on their own. Their neighbors aren’t really aware of what they’re going through,” Welch said. “So having a convening place for the families to be together, they can share their experience and give each other mutual support.”

Dignitaries including U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vermont, center, and U. S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, shovel dirt during a groundbreaking ceremony for the new Vermont Army National Guard Family Readiness Center at Camp Johnson in Colchester on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Since her husband was deployed in June, Kim Buckley said her community has been invaluable. She and her spouse usually divide parenting responsibilities between them, but now she’s managing every ride to sports and trying to provide differing levels of support for both her kids, who have very different needs.
“They don’t always feel seen individually, like it was when Dad and I can just split up duties and give them equal attention,” Buckley said.
Her community has been stepping up around her, offering meals and helping out with transportation, she said.
In an effort to encourage community support, the Vermont National Guard Charitable Foundation recently launched an online service that connects Guard families with Vermonters offering counseling, child care, tax preparation, snowplowing and other assistance.
Sanders asked those attending the ceremony to consider what a deployment means for the children of service members.
“It means that kids suddenly don’t have their dad or their mom at home, and they, in fact, worry whether or not their dad or mom will ever return home and when they will return home,” Sanders said. “That is enormous stress on Vermont families.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: In turnout Tuesday, Democrats outperform Republicans — and 2018
description: New Hampshire’s primary results Tuesday continued a well-worn narrative in the Granite State: Voters chose familiar, household names over insurgent outsiders to lead their parties.  Those include Stefany Shaheen, the Democratic nominee vying against Republican Anthony DiLorenzo for the 1st Congressional District; John E. Sununu, the Republican nominee for U.[...]
text:
In the statewide U.S. Senate primaries, Democrats made up 58.53% of the total voters and Republicans 41.47%, an analysis by the Bulletin shows. (Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin)New Hampshire’s primary results Tuesday continued a well-worn narrative in the Granite State: Voters chose familiar, household names over insurgent outsiders to lead their parties. 
Those include Stefany Shaheen, the Democratic nominee vying against Republican Anthony DiLorenzo for the 1st Congressional District; John E. Sununu, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate; and Chris Pappas, Sununu’s Democratic opponent.
But the results also highlighted another trend. Across the state, Democratic state primary voters outnumbered Republican voters, results from the Associated Press indicated Wednesday afternoon. 
In the statewide U.S. Senate primaries, Democrats made up 58.53% of the total voters and Republicans 41.47%, an analysis by the Bulletin shows. 
A similar split occurred in the 1st Congressional District, long seen as the more competitive of the state’s two congressional districts. Democratic voters in that district made up 57.86% of the share of voters Tuesday and Republicans 42.14%. 
The proportions are based on Associated Press tallies with 97% to 99% of votes counted Wednesday afternoon, and could change when the Secretary of State’s Office certifies the final votes later this week.


The party that does not control the White House historically performs better in midterm elections than the party that does, as voters in the president’s party fall into complacency. 
But Tuesday’s results suggest New Hampshire Democrats also improved their turnout in 2026 when compared to 2018, the last time a Republican president — also Donald Trump — faced a midterm election. 
In 2018, Democrats made up 56.53% of voters in the state primaries for the 1st District, compared to 57.86% on Tuesday. There was no U.S. Senate race in 2018 to compare to 2026. 
In 2018, Pappas and Annie Kuster won the 1st and 2nd Congressional Districts, respectively, and Democrats retook control of the state House and Senate, losing that control in 2020. 
Democrats’ higher share of voters in the primaries do not necessarily mean they will prevail in the general election. Tuesday’s high Democratic voter turnout could be affected by an unusually competitive Democratic race for the 1st District, a seat left vacant by Pappas, and for the open U.S. Senate seat, vacated by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is retiring.
Still, the turnout differences Tuesday — and their similarity to 2018 — could portend challenges for Republicans to flip seats in New Hampshire’s all-Democratic congressional delegation this November, even as Sununu has closed a polling gap with Pappas. An Aug. 26 University of New Hampshire poll found Sununu leading Pappas 45% to 43% in a hypothetical general election matchup, within the 2.1% margin of error. 
The Democrats’ performance defied the predictions of Secretary of State Dave Scanlan, who had predicted a week before the election that Republicans would make up 58.6% of the overall electorate Tuesday. Judging from past elections and voter registration data, Scanlan had predicted 145,751 voters selecting Republican ballots and 103,024 voters selecting Democratic ballots. Instead, with 97% of ballots reported on Wednesday afternoon, 150,684 voters selected Democratic ballots in the U.S. Senate primaries, compared with 106,779 for Republicans.
It is not clear how many Democratic primary voters were undeclared voters, who are allowed to vote in either primary in New Hampshire. 
As of August, Republicans had an advantage in registrations in New Hampshire. Of the 888,475 total registered voters, there were 297,451 registered Republican voters (33.47% of all registered voters), 243,864 registered Democrats (27.45%), and 347,160 registered undeclared voters (39.07%), the Secretary of State’s Office said before the election.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico, Facebook make opening arguments in state’s latest case against social media giant
description: Attorneys for the New Mexico Department of Justice and Facebook made their opening arguments before a Santa Fe jury Wednesday morning as the state’s latest trial against the social media giant began. The trial follows two high-profile courtroom victories for the state in unrelated cases against Meta, Facebook’s parent company.
text:
The New Mexico Department of Justice’s latest trial against Facebook began with opening arguments in Santa Fe on Sept. 9, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Attorneys for the New Mexico Department of Justice and Facebook made their opening arguments before a Santa Fe jury Wednesday morning as the state’s latest trial against the social media giant began.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state initially filed its case against Facebook in 2021, following news reports of the Cambridge Analytica data breach in which users’ personal information was used for political advertisements leading up to the 2016 election. The trial follows two high-profile courtroom victories for the state in unrelated cases against Meta, Facebook’s parent company.
The New Mexico Department of Justice’s attorneys on Wednesday argued that Facebook has long employed a practice of deceiving its users about whether their information is secure and about whether the company sells it to third parties.
That argument is best illustrated through the Cambridge Analytica scandal, attorney Randi McGinn told jurors.
NMDOJ: “Facebook knew things about you that even some of your best friends and family didn’t know”
McGinn described how users typically share their data with third-party apps that operate on Facebook, such as personality quizzes and games like FarmVille. In the case of the Cambridge Analytica scandal, an academic created a personality quiz titled “thisisyourdigitallife” for the consulting firm and posted it to Facebook. In those days, McGinn said, a user who clicked on a third-party application like that often surrendered not only their data, but their Facebook friends’ data, as well.
While only 270,000 people took the survey in question, it exposed the data of more than 87 million people, McGinn said, adding that nearly 350,000 of those people were New Mexicans.
“Facebook knew things about you that even some of your best friends and family didn’t know,” McGinn told jurors.
Cambridge Analytica officials then used that data to aid the campaigns of President Donald Trump and Ted Cruz, McGinn said.
She gave jurors a preview of the evidence she and her colleagues plan to explore over the course of the trial, which is scheduled to run through early October, including video depositions of Mark Zuckerberg and former Facebook Chief Operations Officer Sheryl Sandberg.
McGinn also walked jurors through documents she plans to explore during the trial, including internal email threads in which Zuckerberg and other Facebook executives appear to internally argue over whether they should be honest in public statements about the extent to which the company collects and sells users’ individual data.
She also argued that Facebook’s vacillating stances on countering misinformation — such as instituting a fact-checking program while “whitelisting” accounts like Alex Jones and Andrew Tate — underscore the company’s unreliability.
Facebook counters that state’s argument is ‘frozen’
Facebook’s attorneys quickly countered that hypocrisy clouds the state’s case.
“What you heard was a long speech about how terrible Facebook is,” Dane Butswinkas, an attorney representing Facebook, said to the jury. “You know who is an enormous Facebook user? The State of New Mexico.”
He pointed to Facebook accounts for various state agencies and municipalities in New Mexico and noted that the governmental entities rely on the platform to reach New Mexicans with news, updates about their services and more.
“They didn’t tell you that, did they?” Butswinkas asked.
During his opening arguments, Butswinkas argued that the New Mexico Department of Justice’s attorneys cherry-picked inflammatory details from company records without providing the jury with the full context.
For instance, regarding the internal emails that McGinn showed the jury, he argued that the full email threads show Zuckerberg and other company leaders coming to agreements. As for sharing data, advertisers only receive demographic information of who their ads reach, not personal identifying information, he said. And McGinn’s arguments about content moderation ignore that the company’s digital safeguards prevent the vast majority of objectionable content from ever hitting peoples’ news feeds, he said.
“The details matter,” he said. “Soundbites are not proof.”
Butswinkas contended that Facebook has implemented serious changes since the data breach scandal, which became public nearly a decade ago. After that scandal, the company spent millions investigating the matter and banned about 120 third-party app developers, which were responsible for about 80,000 apps, he said.
“Much of the government’s case is frozen in place,” he said.

title: Trump plan would bar millions of Americans from voting by mail, states tell Supreme Court
text: The Democratic-led states and voting rights groups suing to block enforcement of President Donald Trump’s executive order to restrict mail-in voting warned in briefs to the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday the policy would have disastrous consequences for the upcoming midterm elections if it is allowed to move forward.Less than two months before the Nov. 3 elections, at least two states have already begun sending ballots to voters, and officials in several others have voiced serious concerns that complying with the U.S. Postal Service rule this election cycle is impossible, opponents said.The Democratic attorneys general of 23 states, the District of Columbia and the governor of Pennsylvania told the high court they strongly object to the Trump administration’s request that justices allow the rule to move forward.“Whatever else may be said of USPS’ new rule, it would wreak havoc on States and their voters if it takes effect at this late point—when some States, including North Carolina and Wisconsin, have already begun to mail out ballots,” they wrote.Only Democratic state officials have sought to challenge the rule in court, but Wednesday’s brief noted that top elections officials in the Republican-led states of Utah, Florida and Ohio have also warned the rule would cause “catastrophic harms.”The suit, now at the Supreme Court, was brought by the attorneys general of California, Massachusetts, Nevada, Washington, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Wisconsin, along with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.“Allowing USPS’ new rule to take effect would be virtually certain to prevent many millions of Americans from casting mail ballots in this fall’s elections,” opponents wrote.The record in the Massachusetts federal court that issued the preliminary injunction blocking the rule’s enforcement that the administration is seeking to overturn includes “unrebutted evidence” that “establishes that compliance with USPS’ rule would be impossible ahead of the midterms,” the state officials wrote.Spokespeople for the White House, Postal Service and U.S. Department of Justice, which is representing the Trump administration in the case, did not respond to messages seeking comment Wednesday.The case is on what’s known as the court’s emergency docket, and it’s not clear when a decision on whether or not to keep the preliminary injunction in place will be issued.Voting rights groups echo DemsA coalition of voting rights groups also filed a response Wednesday, making similar arguments.The groups, led by the American Civil Liberties Union, emphasized the likelihood of disenfranchisement for many of the roughly 50 million voters set to receive ballots from the states challenging the rule.Even if the mail specifications under the rule could be met in time for the election, the online portal the Postal Service has rushed to develop is not ready, the challengers wrote. Several friend-of-the-court briefs also made that argument, including the federal employee whistleblower who reported last week that the portal’s rushed development would lead to numerous errors if used this election. As of late last week, states had not yet been given access to the portal, which is supposed to be the mechanism for verifying compliance with the rule, even as some began mailing ballots.“USPS’s Rule gives states mere weeks to implement sweeping changes to their election systems—even though USPS has not yet established the necessary infrastructure to administer its new requirements,” they wrote. “The Rule would disrupt the administration of mail voting mid-election and disenfranchise eligible voters nationwide, including voters in all-mail states like Colorado and Utah and elderly, rural, and disabled voters who must vote by mail.”Beyond Postal Service powerIn addition to the impossibility of states’ complying with the Postal Service rule, which places new requirements on ballot mail and requires states to transmit voter data to the federal government, less than two months before Election Day, the regulation impedes states’ constitutional authorities and oversteps the executive branch’s powers, the state officials and groups wrote.The U.S. Constitution specifies that administering elections is a state responsibility, though Congress may pass laws governing certain elements. The executive branch has virtually no role unless specifically delegated by Congress, the rule’s challengers wrote.And Congress never passed a law to give the Postal Service the kind of power over election mail that the rule claims, they said.“To the contrary, Congress has exhaustively enumerated the types of materials that USPS can lawfully refuse to deliver,” the state officials wrote. “Ballots are not among them.”The rule bans postal workers from delivering ballots that do not meet any of the conditions specified in the rule, including pre-approval of envelope designs and lists of eligible voters that the administration plans to check against a citizenship database maintained by the Department of Homeland Security.Outsiders weigh inA flurry of 17 friend-of-the-court briefs hit the Supreme Court docket Tuesday and Wednesday. None sided with the administration.The briefs, representing bipartisan former governors, state and local election officials, military voters, the Postal Service workers’ union, good government organizations, Democratic campaign groups and others all said the rule was impossible to comply with at this point in the election cycle.“The late-breaking USPS Final Rule—which was promulgated mere months before the November 3, 2026 general midterm elections, and which mandates sweeping, costly, and burdensome changes to mail-in voting procedures—would prove disastrous for election officials and election administration,” local officials and the pro-democracy group Center for Election Innovation wrote. “And it would seriously undermine the upcoming elections.”In another filing, a bipartisan group of current and former local and state election officials said it was impossible to comply with the rule this year. Their brief noted that many of their members were Republicans or represented Republican-majority districts and emphasized that they took no position on the rule’s legality. But they said implementing it now was infeasible and ran afoul of a Supreme Court principle that changes in election policy should not happen during or close to an election.“The principle rests on incontestable facts about voters and about the people who run elections: that late changes breed confusion, that confusion keeps eligible voters from voting, and that a chaotic election erodes confidence in the result,” they wrote. They “therefore suggest only this: that the November 3, 2026 general election be conducted under the rules that were in place when the election’s administration began.”

title: Frederick Lack Sawabini
description:
Fred grew up with his siblings, Wadi Jr., Stuart and Julia, in a loving home that embraced everything Vermont had to offer: skiing the Green Mountains in winter, and summers of sailing and water-skiing on Lake Champlain.

text:
Born: 10/31/1951
Burlington
Died: 09/05/2026
Details of service:
A memorial service will be held at 10:00 a.m. on Friday, September 18, 2026, at the Charlotte Congregational Church, 403 Church Hill Road, Charlotte, Vermont. In lieu of flowers, gifts may be made in Fred’s memory to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute to support cancer research, online at dana-farber.org/gift or by mail to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, P.O. Box 849168, Boston, MA 02284.

Frederick Lack Sawabini passed away peacefully on Saturday, September 5, 2026, surrounded by his family, after a long battle with myelofibrosis. He was 74.
Fred was born on October 31, 1951, in Burlington to Dr. Wadi Issa Sawabini and Harriet Colgate “Abbe” Lack Sawabini. His father was born in Jaffa, Palestine, and came to America during the Second World War. Abbe graduated from Smith College and met Wadi in Vermont while serving the Episcopal Church. Fred grew up with his siblings, Wadi Jr., Stuart and Julia, in a loving home that embraced everything Vermont had to offer: skiing the Green Mountains in winter, and summers of sailing and water-skiing on Lake Champlain.
Fred graduated from Eaglebrook School and Phillips Academy Andover, where he met Gay Luster, a student at Abbot Academy. He went on to graduate from Williams College. Fred and Gay married in 1985 and raised three children together in Wilton, Connecticut.
Fred began his career at D’Arcy Masius Benton & Bowles in New York, rising to Vice President. Excited by the challenge of building a new venture, he next raised the financing to build a ceramic tile factory in Idaho. After selling the factory, Fred went on to spend a decade at Channel One News, opening the company’s office in Hong Kong before returning to New York as President of Sales and Marketing. He closed his career as a Senior Vice President at Viacom and CBS.
In 2017 Fred left New York, first for Connecticut and then home to Vermont, settling in Shelburne. He skied the Green Mountains and took a series of motorcycle trips with his son. He played guitar, rode his bicycles and got out on Lake Champlain whenever he could. Even in his final weeks he was riding 20 miles at a stretch and boating on the lake.
Fred is survived by his children, Alex, James (Gaurie), and Polly; his grandchildren, Elizabeth (“Eliza”) and Peter; his siblings, Wadi Jr. (Mary) and Julia (Jeanne); his sister-in-law Nicoline, Stuart’s wife; his nieces and nephews: Wadi Jr. and Mary’s children, Issa (Erica), Annie, and Jake (Meg), and Stuart and Nicoline’s daughters, Kathryn (Dan) and Abigail (Ryan); and many beloved cousins and friends. He was predeceased by his parents, Wadi and Abbe, and by his brother, Stuart.
The family is deeply grateful to Carol Georges, whose companionship and devoted care brought Fred comfort and joy in his final year.

title: States sue feds over endangered species rollbacks
description: A coalition of state attorneys general filed a pair of lawsuits Wednesday challenging the Trump administration’s rollbacks of protections for endangered species.  The lawsuits, filed by 20 states and the District of Columbia, seek to reinstate rules that protect the habitat that endangered species depend on to survive.  Under President Donald Trump, federal[...]
text:
A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologist examines macroinvertebrates at the National Elk Refuge near Jackson Hole, Wyoming. A coalition of 21 attorneys general sued the agency Wednesday over rollbacks to the Endangered Species Act. (Photo by Kari Cieszkiewicz/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)A coalition of state attorneys general filed a pair of lawsuits Wednesday challenging the Trump administration’s rollbacks of protections for endangered species. 
The lawsuits, filed by 20 states and the District of Columbia, seek to reinstate rules that protect the habitat that endangered species depend on to survive. 
Under President Donald Trump, federal agencies have changed their interpretation of “harm” under the endangered species law to include only actions that directly injure or kill animals. For decades, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and other federal agencies had taken a broader position that the law also banned the destruction of forests, streams and wetlands that those animals depend on for nesting, mating and raising young. 
“The federal government’s attempt to gut the Endangered Species Act threatens the habitats of orcas, sockeye salmon, and other endangered species that are part of our economy, culture, and way of life,” Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, a Democrat, said in a news release. 
The feds no longer protect endangered species habitat. States say they can’t pick up the slack.

A second lawsuit challenges a pair of new rules that change the process for federal wildlife officials to designate “critical habitat.” The rules reduce protections for newly listed threatened species and make it easier for officials to decline to list certain lands as critical. 
“For over half a century, the (Endangered Species Act) has stood as a bipartisan example of what it means to protect an irreplaceable part of our planet, but these new rules attempt to destroy longstanding and integral regulatory protections and open the door to further species decline and possible extinctions,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement. 
The lawsuits argue that the rollbacks enacted by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service violate two key federal laws, the Administrative Procedure Act and the National Environmental Policy Act. According to Bonta’s press release, the rules ignore not just the purpose and history of the Endangered Species Act but also numerous court rulings and the law’s “overall precautionary approach.”
The lawsuits are led by Brown and Bonta, along with the attorneys general of Maryland and Massachusetts. The suits were also joined by the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Wisconsin. 
The lawsuits were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.
In a statement, the Department of the Interior vowed to “vigorously defend its authority” to manage endangered species under the new guidelines.
“This lawsuit seeks to preserve a decades-old regulatory overreach that expanded the Endangered Species Act beyond the authority granted by Congress,” the agency said, according to Reuters.

title: Audit: Minnesota often fails to inspect assisted living facilities on time
description: A Minnesota assisted living facility was able to score average ratings from the state on resident health, safety and staffing, despite five separate incidents in two years that led to one resident death and four hospitalizations. That’s because the Minnesota Department of Human Services doesn’t factor in serious maltreatment incidents when publishing an assi[...]
text:
Deputy Legislative Auditor Jodi Munson Rodriguez and Legislative Auditor Judy Randall present a report to a joint hearing of the House education finance and children and families committees on Feb. 8, 2023. Randall's office presented a report on assisted living facilities Wednesday. (Photo by Catherine Davis/House Information Services)A Minnesota assisted living facility was able to score average ratings from the state on resident health, safety and staffing, despite five separate incidents in two years that led to one resident death and four hospitalizations.
That’s because the Minnesota Department of Human Services doesn’t factor in serious maltreatment incidents when publishing an assisted living facility “report card” rating, according to a new report from the Office of the Legislative Auditor.
The legislative auditor, a nonpartisan watchdog in the legislative branch, evaluated the licensing process for the over 2,000 assisted living facilities that provide housing and medical services to seniors and disabled adults in Minnesota and also found the state is frequently late on its routine inspections of assisted living facilities.
“We have basically a simple recommendation that the department comply with the statutorily required timelines for assisted living facility inspections,” said David Kirchner, the manager for the evaluation, during a Wednesday presentation to legislators.
Minnesota established licensing for assisted living facilities in 2021 following a string of maltreatment investigations — becoming the last state to do so, KARE 11 reported at the time.
Assisted living facilities, state-regulated businesses sometimes referred to as “group homes,” can look like converted single-family homes with just a handful of residents, or large buildings that can serve sometimes hundreds of people. They differ from nursing homes, which are meant for people with higher medical needs and have to meet federal standards. The distinction in use is sometimes blurry, though, with seniors increasingly opting into assisted living homes over nursing homes, the Star Tribune reported.
Regulating assisted living facilities is complex: the state’s health department is responsible for licensing, while the human services department is responsible for paying facilities that have clients on Medicaid. A third regulatory body oversees licensing individual assisted living facility directors.


The Office of the Legislative Auditor found that, for the most part, the state “did a good job processing licensing applications.”
But it also found that health department inspectors completed their first two-year round of routine inspections a year late.
Health department leaders explained in a response to the report that the delay was caused in part by an unexpectedly high number of applications and many of its nurses being reassigned during COVID. Auditors noted that inspections have sped up since then, though in the latest data from the first half of 2025, still less than a third of inspections were completed by the statutory deadline.
Health department inspectors also investigate facilities that have complaints of neglect or abuse, and the health department regularly publishes substantiated maltreatment complaints. A recent MPR News investigation found that some assisted living facilities faced minimal consequences in cases of substantiated maltreatment.



How licensing has affected the amount of maltreatment in facilities was out of the scope of the new report, Kirchner said, though auditors did find that substantiated cases of maltreatment don’t hurt a facility’s rating.
Ratings of facilities have been published in report cards by the Department of Human Services since 2024 and are meant to help people find quality providers for themselves or their loved ones. Maltreatment findings are listed in the report card separately from a facility’s rating out of five stars.
Department of Human Services Temporary Commissioner John Connolly said that a facility’s rating “ideally would reflect” maltreatment findings, and that developing a system that properly incorporates maltreatment in the same scale as the existing rating system is doable but would take time.
Medicaid spending on assisted living facilities was around $1.1 billion in the 2024 fiscal year, according to the report. For context, that same year, Minnesota spent $18.5 billion on its entire Medicaid program.
Reports of Medicaid fraud and, by extension, the ongoing state-federal fight over federal Medicaid funding, have centered on 14 services deemed vulnerable to fraud, waste and abuse by the state. That list does not include assisted living services, called “customized living” in the state’s Medicaid program.
Still, auditors highlighted a possible “risk for incorrect payments”: DHS doesn’t check a facility’s maximum capacity when paying claims. Auditors cited one facility which had a licensed capacity of six residents but was paid for 18 residents during a single month in 2024.
Echoing a much-used sentiment in official communications, Department of Health Deputy Commissioner Wendy Underwood said at the Wednesday presentation: “Fighting fraud is everyone’s job at our agency.”

name: VTDigger
title: Federal judge blocks Vermont AG’s probe of ‘Planet Hank’ AI video
description:
The ruling tested Vermont’s first attempt to enforce its new synthetic-media law, finding that a controversial AI-generated video was protected political satire.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Federal judge blocks Vermont AG’s probe of ‘Planet Hank’ AI video.
text:
U.S. District Court Judge William Sessions speaks at the Vermont Statehouse in September 2018. File photo by Mike Dougherty/VTDigger

A political satire video was “ridiculous” enough to be protected speech, a federal judge ruled, blocking Vermont’s first attempt to enforce its new AI-media law.
“The Court considers this video to have a ridiculous nature and finds that Vermont’s interest in protecting and preserving the integrity of the electoral process and related fraud is lower when the threat faced is an unrealistic, satirical video,” Senior U.S. District Judge William K. Sessions III wrote in a decision issued Tuesday.
The preliminary injunction marks the first major court test of Act 75, enacted in March to regulate deceptive AI-generated election material. Although the ruling applies only to one video and does not resolve a broader challenge to the law, it raises questions about how Vermont can regulate synthetic political media without infringing on constitutionally protected satire.
Sessions ordered Attorney General Charity Clark’s office not to enforce a civil investigative demand against Hank Poitras, who posts videos and political commentary under the name “Planet Hank,” or take other enforcement action against him based on a video he uploaded to several social media platforms entitled “Mark Helps Vermont Take Out The Trash,” generated using artificial intelligence.
Sessions found that Poitras was likely to prove Clark’s investigation violated his First Amendment rights. The judge also found that the video appeared to qualify for Act 75’s exemption for satire and parody.
The law requires certain synthetic media that injures a political candidate’s reputation and is published within 90 days of an election to include a disclaimer identifying it as digitally manipulated or generated. Poitras posted his video without a disclaimer two months before Vermont’s Aug. 11 primary, which fell within the timespan that requires such a disclosure.
But Sessions concluded that the video’s voice-over, the “unnatural appearances” of the people depicted and the events of the video all contributed to an unmistakably satirical character.
Sen. Brian Collamore, R-Rutland, who sponsored the legislation in the Vermont Senate, said Sessions’ ruling reflected lawmakers’ intent.
“One of the provisions was an exemption to the law if it was clearly satirical,” Collamore said, adding that he thought most reasonable people would consider Poitras’ video satirical. “It did not have to have identification as AI generated.”
Poitras posted the video on June 7. It uses AI-generated likenesses of U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., and then-Republican U.S. House candidate Mark Coester.
In the video, Coester criticizes Balint’s campaign and policies before using an excavator to lift her into a trash bin outside the Vermont Statehouse.
“Help fight back against evil,” a narrator says. “Help Vermont take out the trash.”
Five days later, the attorney general’s office notified Poitras that it was investigating whether the video violated Act 75. The office offered to close the investigation at the time if Poitras brought the video into compliance with the law by adding a disclosure, according to court documents.
Poitras instead sued Clark on July 8, contending that the demand that he alter his video under the threat of civil or criminal penalties violated his First Amendment rights.
Coester, who later lost the Republican primary to Gerald Malloy, said in an interview Wednesday that the investigation was unjustified even though the video also could have reflected poorly on him.
“It’s just really sad that it’s the citizens that pay the price for legislation that’s unconstitutional in the first place,” Coester said. “This has cost a high price for people to defend against something they never should have been prosecuted on, something that was clearly satire.”
Poitras’ lawsuit challenges Act 75 more broadly, alleging five First Amendment violations and one violation of the 14th Amendment. Sessions’ preliminary injunction is considerably narrower: It applies only to the June 7 video and the attorney general’s resulting investigative demand.
Lauren Jandl, Clark’s chief of staff, said the office was reviewing the decision and “determining next steps.”
“The Attorney General’s Office supported the synthetic media disclosure law because transparency and the integrity of elections are critical,” Jandl wrote in an email.
Poitras and his attorneys intend to seek a permanent injunction preventing Clark from enforcing Act 75 against Poitras and others, Poitras’ attorney Brady Toensing said.
“This preliminary injunction is an important victory for our fundamental right to make fun of politicians in this country,” Toensing wrote in an email.

title: Mental health professionals highlight errors in Nebraska assessment for developmentally disabled
description: LINCOLN — Just over a year after Nebraska launched a new system to assess Nebraskans with intellectual and developmental disabilities seeking Medicaid assistance, a group of parents gathered to inform state officials about the negative impacts the change has had on their families. text:
Tony Green, director of the Division of Developmental Disabilities in the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, at a meeting of the Nebraska Olmstead Advisory Committee. Dec. 19, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Just over a year after Nebraska launched a new system to assess Nebraskans with intellectual and developmental disabilities seeking Medicaid assistance, a group of parents gathered to inform state officials about the negative impacts the change has had on their families.
Mental health professionals Carol Salber and Tori Sorensen, who are both parents of participants in the system, gave a presentation Wednesday to Nebraska’s Developmental Disabilities Advisory Committee that noted multiple flaws in the state’s interRAI tool.
The interRAI system determines the level of publicly assisted care, services and funding for Nebraskans with developmental disability waivers. Salber and Sorensen’s presentation identified seven errors in how the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services calculates what each participant receives, which they claimed could dramatically shift the funding and services doled out.
InterRAI uses a Case Mix Index chart to help measure what funding tier a participant should land in based on the complexity of their circumstance. Sorensen said Nebraska officials made several typos copying the Case Mix Index, and some of those errors impact both funding and eligibility of services for participants.
One example in their presentation claimed that the errors could result in a participant receiving nearly $68,000 that they don’t need, while a different participant who is in need would lose out on that same amount.
“If the interRAI is wrong, then I have even more questions about it being a valid test,” Sorensen said. “If Nebraska is wrong, then we need to fix it. Because certain individuals are getting less funding, significantly less funding, just because of a typo.”
DHHS spokesman Jeff Powell said the department would review the concerns shared at Wednesday’s meeting. He noted that assessments that result in a reduced funding tier automatically undergo a secondary review, and he said assessments can be corrected and rescored when concerns are identified.
“DHHS will continue to monitor the system and use the independent review to identify any areas where improvements may be needed,” Powell said in an email.

Sorensen and Salber listed multiple other issues with interRAI, including that the state’s transition to the system altered the funding of 46% of continued participants. According to their presentation, 17% of participants saw their funding decrease by at least one tier.
Salber said this change has resulted in participants with significantly different needs being categorized in the same funding tiers. She gave an example of a participant who took the children’s version of the interRAI assessment and was placed in a basic funding tier. The following year, the same participant completed the adult interRAI assessment and was placed in the advanced tier, despite having no major health changes.
One of the biggest flaws noted at Wednesday’s meeting was that the interRAI system lowered the funding of participants who live at home with their loved ones. Salber said this is considered “informal support” and is used to justify reduced aid.
Multiple parents testified Wednesday that their children’s funding tiers dropped because of this factor, though all said their needs are severe enough to require higher support.
Nancy Enstrom, a 74-year-old mother from Dodge County, said she has kept her 51-year-old daughter alive by caring for her at home, although doctors had told her she wouldn’t survive past infancy. Her daughter’s funding tier decreased after the switch to interRAI, and Enstrom said she was told by state officials that her daughter would be in the advanced tier if she didn’t live at home.
Enstrom said she is suing the state to restore the previous level of support.
“You will not be the people that ruin my daughter’s life,” Enstrom said.
Enstrom said her husband works 80-90 hours a week so she can stay home and care for their daughter. She said she hasn’t made a penny off the aid they have received from the state.
Kathy Rohloff, a mother whose 15-year-old son fell two funding tiers in the switch to interRAI, argued that parents who care for their disabled children at home are more cost-effective for the state. She estimated that housing the same participants at a state institution would be roughly four times more expensive than allowing parents to care for them.
Enstrom agreed, estimating that parents like her and Rohloff have saved Nebraska millions of dollars over the years. Rohloff said parents don’t want to walk away from their children, but argued that the new system encourages that.
DHHS officials announced in August that they hired an outside contractor to review interRAI usage. Tony Green, DHHS Division of Disability and Aging director, said he doesn’t anticipate receiving the report until next spring.
Mike Browne, vice chair of the committee, asked if DHHS could halt making reductions in funding until after the report. He said he viewed some of the concerns expressed Wednesday as a fairness issue.
“I see a real potential problem, because it looks like you’re dividing into two classes,” Browne said.
Green disagreed with Browne’s perspective, saying regardless of a participant’s guardians, the same review happens for each participant. He said DHHS would not pause its implementation of interRAI, as it would create a budget concern to continue funding increases under the system while pausing any reductions.

title: Alaska continues rollout of Rural Health Transformation Program awards
description: Alaska Department of Health officials announced a fifth round of federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding awards on Friday. The latest awards for $25.8 million bring the total to more than $207 million to date. The funding is aimed at bolstering Alaska’s rural health system. The latest round of awards will go to 32 projects […]
text:
The Providence Kodiak Island Medical Center, Kodiak's main hospital, is seen on Feb. 2, 2024. The hospital facility is owned by the Kodiak Island Borough who was awarded $3.8 million in September 2026 to update the hospital's climate control system. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaska Department of Health officials announced a fifth round of federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding awards on Friday. The latest awards for $25.8 million bring the total to more than $207 million to date.
The funding is aimed at bolstering Alaska’s rural health system. The latest round of awards will go to 32 projects focused on improving health access, nutrition, telehealth services, healthcare infrastructure, workforce development and more. 
Alaska was awarded $272 million in federal funding under the program this year, with the remaining roughly $65 million expected to be awarded in the coming weeks, ahead of a federal deadline of October 30.
Congress created the Rural Health Transformation Program last year as part of the Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act to offset the fallout from the bill’s nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid spending cuts over the next decade — particularly in rural communities. The $50 billion in program funding is set to be allocated over the next five years, until 2030. Alaska is one of the largest recipients and is slated to receive roughly $1.3 billion.
