title: The largest US school districts restrict student AI use
description: The country’s two largest school districts — New York City and Los Angeles — banned most student use of artificial intelligence in classrooms for this school year as anxiety over AI’s effect on learning intensifies. The Los Angeles Unified School District announced last week that it is barring student use of generative AI on school-issued […]
text:
Students work in a classroom. The nation's two largest school districts banned AI use for most students this school year. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The country’s two largest school districts — New York City and Los Angeles — banned most student use of artificial intelligence in classrooms for this school year as anxiety over AI’s effect on learning intensifies.
The Los Angeles Unified School District announced last week that it is barring student use of generative AI on school-issued devices for the current school year. Generative AI creates new text, images or other content following a user’s instructions. During the school year, a committee will produce recommendations for use of the technology in future years.
New York City Public Schools last week announced a similar but less broad approach. The district put in place a one-year moratorium on generative AI for children from pre-kindergarten through eighth grade. 
Schools spend billions on AI, but struggle to figure out what’s worth buying

High school students will have to complete 45-minute AI literacy modules twice a year. Some career-focused AI use will be allowed and some high schools will be permitted to test AI pilot programs.
The restrictions, which New York officials said will affect 600,000 students, will allow time to study the technology’s impacts. 
“The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a news release. “We do not see it that way.” 
Chicago officials may follow suit. About half the candidates running for the Chicago Board of Education this November have signed a pledge calling for a three-year moratorium on generative AI use in the public school classrooms.
Smaller school districts around the country have taken similar steps. Districts in Colorado, Kansas, Minnesota, Texas and Washington have blocked or limited tools such as ChatGPT, while some allow approved platforms under teacher supervision.

title: Your vote. Your child’s classroom. Your electric bill. Your water. Your health.

It is supposed to protect our constitutional rights when politicians overreach. And it is supposed to be a place where every North Carolinian can get […]
text:
The North Carolina Supreme Court building, pictured on June 2, 2026. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)As the North Carolina Supreme Court begins a new session, we need to remember what this court is supposed to be. It is supposed to be a check on power. It is supposed to protect our constitutional rights when politicians overreach. And it is supposed to be a place where every North Carolinian can get a fair hearing.
That matters more today than ever.
More than 95% of cases in this country are handled by state courts. And as the U.S. Supreme Court pushes fundamental questions about our freedoms back to the states, state courts and state constitutions are increasingly important protectors of our rights.
But those protections only mean something if the judges sitting on our Supreme Court are willing to enforce them.
And for my family, this is personal. My daughter Ella was one of the North Carolina voters whose ballots were challenged after the 2024 Supreme Court election. Ella was a lawful voter. She was living and teaching abroad in Spain. She followed the rules. She cast her ballot. And months after the election, this court was willing to let her lawful vote be thrown out.
My daughter had to become a plaintiff in a federal class action lawsuit to protect her vote and the votes of other North Carolinians. Ultimately, a federal court stepped in and protected those voters. Think about that. North Carolinians had to turn to a federal court to protect their votes from their own state Supreme Court.
And voting rights aren’t the only place where this court’s decisions hit home for my family.
I have two adult children who went through North Carolina’s underfunded public schools. And now I have a young daughter, Anya, in the same schools. For two years, Anya spent nearly half the school year without a permanent classroom teacher.
Think about what that means for a child. Months without the stability of a teacher who knows her, knows where she is struggling, and knows what she needs to learn. And all the while, our state Constitution promises her something very different.
The Leandro case established that every North Carolina child has a constitutional right to a sound, basic education. Yet decades later, families like mine are still waiting for North Carolina to fulfill that promise.
My daughter cannot get those years back.
That is what I want people to understand about the decisions made in this building.
These cases aren’t abstract legal arguments. They become classrooms without teachers. They become children falling behind. They become parents lying awake at night wondering whether their child is getting the education the Constitution says she has a right to receive. And they become lawful voters like my daughter Ella having to go to federal court to fight to make sure their votes count.
But it goes far beyond my family.
The decisions made here can determine who has political power. In 2023, this Supreme Court reversed its own previous ruling on partisan gerrymandering and cleared the way for the legislature to draw new congressional and legislative maps. Those maps determine which communities are kept together, which are divided, and ultimately whose voices have power in Raleigh and Washington.
And the decisions made here can determine something as basic as the water we drink and the health care we can access. When this court begins its new session on September 8, it will confront cases involving health care benefits for state retirees and contamination from forever chemicals in North Carolina’s water.
That is why North Carolina For The People created Why Judges Matter NC, a resource to help North Carolinians understand our courts, the judges who serve on them, and why judicial elections deserve our attention.
And there are other trusted, nonpartisan resources to help voters prepare for the 2026 election. Democracy NC’s NC Voter offers information about candidates, voting rules and how to cast your ballot. NC Voter Guide from Common Cause North Carolina provides information about candidates and what is on the ballot. VOTE411, from the League of Women Voters Education Fund, provides personalized ballot information, candidate information and voting rules to help voters prepare to cast their ballot.
Before you vote, learn about the courts, learn about the candidates and make a plan to cast your ballot.
Your vote. Your child’s classroom. Your electric bill. Your drinking water. Your health care.
That is the power of a state Supreme Court. These decisions have consequences. That is why judicial elections matter.
Melissa Price Kromm is executive director of North Carolina For The People and N.C. For The People Action.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Congress must ensure Pell Grants for Mississippi students, college access advocate says
description: View of the University of Southern Mississippi campus, Wednesday, Nov. 12, 2025, in Hattiesburg.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.

It is back to school season, and over 67,000 college students in Mississippi are relying on Pell Grants to help pay for college. But, the program is facing a $15 billion funding shortfall that will undermine college access and success unless the United States Congress fixes the funding gap. 
The Pell Grant program is the primary federal grant helping low- and middle-income students pay for college. Students can use the funds to pay for tuition, books and living costs like rent and food.  
Congress wisely made structural changes to the Pell Grant program at the end of the first Trump administration as part of the FAFSA Simplification Act. Those changes created a new Student Aid Index, based on family income and assets, that is used to determine how much financial aid a student is eligible for. The changes raised the eligibility threshold for Pell Grants, making almost 600,000 more students eligible, and approximately 1.7 million more eligible for the maximum grant. 
The eligibility changes mean more students are receiving Pell than anticipated. Because Pell is funded through discretionary appropriations, Congress must estimate how much money is needed. When the estimates are too low, there is a shortfall that requires additional appropriations. 
Mississippians who rely on Pell funding need to know that funding will be there for the duration of their programs. Students cannot make informed decisions about postsecondary education and training if they do not know whether the financial aid they are counting on will be available from one year to the next.
Cuts to Pell would also undermine Mississippi’s ongoing efforts to increase postsecondary credentials and degrees that lead to family-sustaining employment. 
Mississippi Valley State University is seen on Wednesday, March 4, 2026, in Itta Bena. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Just last year, the state expanded eligibility for financial aid programs like the Higher Ed Legislative Plan and Mississippi Tuition Assistance Grant to make it easier for our students to get help paying for college. But, state financial aid relies on complementing Pell funding, not replacing it. If Pell grants are reduced, state funding cannot make up the difference.  
Mississippi has also been a leader in helping students apply for financial aid to help pay for college. This year, according to the National College Attainment Network’s FAFSA Tracker, Mississippi ranks third in the country with a record-breaking 71% of the 2026 high school class completing the aid application. FAFSA is the federal form that determines student eligibility for aid to help pay for college and other training after high school. 
More students, especially low-income and first-generation students, enrolling in college is a good problem to have.
FAFSA simplification and increased Pell Grant eligibility are rare examples of policy changes rapidly achieving the hoped-for outcome of increasing college access. This progress will be undermined if Congress jeopardizes millions of students’ Pell Grants by failing to fully fund the program.
There are positive signs that this administration and congress are willing to fix the Pell shortfall. The President’s budget proposed maintaining the current maximum grant, but did not include funding to address the shortfall. Congress is now considering legislation that would both address the funding gap and increase the maximum grant by $50.
But, the House proposal would pay for that increase by eliminating subsidized federal student loans, another important tool that helps make college affordable. This approach would add thousands of dollars of interest to the loan balances of millions of student loan borrowers, but especially students who rely on Pell funding. 
The maximum Pell Grant of $7,395 is already too low. Today, the max grant covers 30% of average tuition, housing and food at public colleges, down from 79% of those expenses in 1975. If the maximum grant had kept pace with inflation since 2022, when it was last increased, it would be $8,109 today. An extra $50 is a positive if insufficient step in the right direction. 
If Congress fails to address the Pell funding shortfall, millions of students will struggle to cover tuition, possibly stop attending school or decide not to enroll in the first place 
Financial challenges are already the primary reason that students leave college. There is also strong evidence that every $1,000 of grant aid increases graduation rates by 1.5 percentage points. Similar sized cuts are likely to reduce graduation rates, after years of positive gains. 
Lower graduation rates would disproportionally impact first generation and low-income students, potentially reversing the enrollment gains we are seeing among those groups. 
They are the students that we work to support at the Woodward Hines Education Foundation and our Get2College program, and who have the most to gain from higher education and training. Those students know exactly how valuable college is, because they know what it’s like when a lack of education limits your options. 
Mississippi students are doing their part. They are completing the FAFSA, enrolling in college and pursuing credentials that can strengthen their futures and our state’s workforce. They should be able to count on the financial aid they planned around.
Congress must close the Pell funding shortfall so Mississippi students can move forward knowing the support they planned on will be there when they need it most.

James E. McHale is president and CEO of the Woodward Hines Education Foundation and the Mississippi Higher Education Assistance Corporation, based in Jackson. Since joining WHEF as president in December 2015, McHale has led the organization’s efforts to expand postsecondary access, affordability, persistence and completion and strengthen connections between education and family-sustaining work for Mississippians.
Under McHale’s leadership, WHEF has expanded its work beyond college access to support promising practices, programs and policies that help more Mississippians enter and complete postsecondary education and connect their credentials to meaningful employment. He has led efforts to strengthen WHEF’s college access program, Get2College, which provides free college planning and financial aid assistance to students and families across Mississippi, while also advancing the foundation’s partnerships and policy work to address systemic barriers to postsecondary success.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri counties suffered ballot shortages amid high primary turnout
description: When Kelli Knapp went to vote during the Aug. 4 primary, she was surprised to find a long line of people waiting outside Hawthorn Hill Elementary School in Lee’s Summit. Her husband, who was ahead of her in line, texted her after about 20 minutes of waiting that the poll workers had run out of […]
text:
Hawthorn Hill Elementary School was one of the polling locations that ran out of preprinted ballots during the Aug. 4 primary, causing long waits.(Vaughn Wheat/The Beacon).When Kelli Knapp went to vote during the Aug. 4 primary, she was surprised to find a long line of people waiting outside Hawthorn Hill Elementary School in Lee’s Summit.
Her husband, who was ahead of her in line, texted her after about 20 minutes of waiting that the poll workers had run out of preprinted Democratic ballots. Once Knapp got to the front, they were out of nonpartisan ballots as well.
Voters could use the electronic voting machine authorized under the Americans With Disabilities Act, but that also had a 30-minute plus wait. Knapp, who was on carpool duty that day, ended up voting on a Republican ballot for various issues before she had to leave.
The long wait and inability to vote for the candidates she wanted made it a scary and frustrating process, Knapp said.
“It felt like there was a restriction on our ability to access” voting, Knapp said.
Van Wiley Jr., another voter at Hawthorn Hill, said he arrived at the polls around 5 p.m. but additional ballots didn’t arrive until closer to 7 p.m., the time the polls were scheduled to close.
“Somebody finally came to deliver Democratic ballots, and so it was a kind of a little scramble,” Wiley said. “Everybody just grabbed one, you just waited for the guy or the lady ahead of you to finish, and then they passed the pen back to you.”
Hawthorn Hill wasn’t the only polling location in Jackson County that ran out of preprinted ballots that day. Fifty-eight out of 103 polling places ran out of some type of ballot, with almost all needing additional nonpartisan ballots.
Hawthorn Hill and Holy Spirit Church were the only two that needed additional preprinted Democrat ballots.
Other counties across the state had similar experiences.
In Pulaski County, preprinted nonpartisan and party-affiliated ballots ran out across some of the county’s smaller polling locations, County Clerk David Ernst said. He said it was the first time it had happened in his eight years of experience.
Callaway County Clerk Ronda Miller said in an email that half of the 18 polling locations in the county ran out of nonpartisan paper ballots, adding that they had never had that many people wanting to vote nonpartisan before.
In each case, voters had access to an ADA machine if they wanted to vote nonpartisan or Democrat.
The culprit for the shortages across all of these counties was higher-than-expected voter turnout.
Statewide Democratic turnout — calculated using the state auditor’s race — saw almost 160,000 more people casting votes than in the 2022 primary, an increase of 49.5%. Republican turnout also saw a boost, with over 58,000 more votes cast in the primary this year than in  2022, an increase of almost 10%.
Jackson County alone saw over 16,000 more Democratic ballots and over 4,000 more nonpartisan ballots cast than in the 2024 August primary.
As voters remained frustrated and wary about a similar situation happening in November, election officials pointed to the difficulties in determining turnout and laid out a plan for improvements.
 The art of election turnout prediction

Determining voter turnout uses a mix of prior data and a little bit of guesswork.
Election authorities use turnout numbers from previous primaries and elections to predict how many ballots will be needed.
However, big races or issues, like the constitutional amendments Missourians voted on, can easily throw off those numbers as more motivated voters go to the polls.
For example, primary turnout in Jackson County typically sits between 26% and 30% of registered voters, or about 68,000 people at the high end. The 2026 primary saw nearly 88,000 people cast votes, representing 35.5% of registered voters.
Chris Mann, the research director at the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said preprinted ballot shortages aren’t entirely unusual because of those fluctuations.
“It’s not common, but it’s not unexpected,” Mann said. “There’s an art in looking at elections. If you’ve got a big high-profile race that’s spending a lot of money, that might drive turnout in the way the last one didn’t.”
The Jackson County Election Board initially ordered 107,610 ballots, costing roughly $38,300. That breaks down into 49,585 Democratic ballots, 54,195 Republican ballots, 965 Libertarian and 2,865 nonpartisan ballots.
JCEB Co-director Sara Zorich said the board had ordered more ballots overall this year in anticipation of more people turning out to vote on the constitutional amendments.
“It’s not that we didn’t recognize,” Zorich said. “We were doing what we thought was enough, and obviously we fell a little bit short.”
It ended up ordering 4,300 additional ballots, most of which were nonpartisan, and 20 additional machines as precincts reported shortages.
Tyler Spencer, the other co-director for JCEB, said in an email that primaries in particular can be difficult to plan for because there are multiple ballot types available. He said they don’t want to overprint in any one category and waste resources, especially since Jackson County has 247,018 registered voters.
“Ordering enough of every ballot type for every registered voter would mean ordering over 988,000 ballots,” Spencer said. “That would create a significant amount of unnecessary printing expense and waste, which is why (we) use historical turnout and ballot selection to determine reasonable quantities.”
Even if the board had elected to print one of each of the four types of ballots based off of previous peak voter turnout of 68,000 ballots cast, it would have resulted in roughly 184,400 unused ballots. That would have cost the county roughly $66,240.
By party, that would have roughly broken down into 21,000 unused Democratic ballots, 33,000 unused Republican ballots, 67,600 unused Libertarian ballots and 63,000 unused nonpartisan ballots.
Missouri’s open primary system can also make estimating particularly difficult, Mann said. While someone might be registered as a Republican, there’s nothing prohibiting them from taking a Democratic or nonpartisan ballot.
“How many people are going to show up for the Democratic primary to vote a nonpartisan ballot about nonpartisan questions, and how many are going to show up for the Republican primary?” Mann said. “So there’s just more uncertainty there, which increases the likelihood that they get one of those estimates incorrect.”
That was part of what happened in Jackson County. Spencer said the board heard from voters who normally identify with one party but chose the other party’s ballot because they were interested in particular races.
But missing the estimate can result in long waits, frustration and, for some, the inability to vote.
“It is true that someone might have to leave the line because they have childcare or work, and so that cost can be real, and it can mean that people lose the opportunity to vote,” Mann said. “But the system has fail-safes to try to ensure that everyone can be able to vote.”
Missing the estimate can also have repercussions for future elections.
 Voter confidence for November

Mistakes can rattle voter confidence.
The August primary shortages came at a time when the country is already seeing increased election worries. American confidence in election fairness and accuracy has fallen to 55%, according to the Pew Research Center. That’s the lowest rating since the start of the 2020s.
Because of that, everything is under heightened scrutiny, Mann said. But he stressed that poll workers are still human and mistakes happen, and the important takeaway is to make sure it doesn’t become a pattern.
“Making a mistake over and over again is a very different level of accountability for not doing their job correctly. But in some ways, the fact that this is a bit of a novel story tells you that this is something that happened in this primary because there’s something (else) going on,” Mann said. “This is an important thing to shine the light on, but also to shine the light of ‘this is an honest mistake.’”
Tyler McCall, executive director for the Jackson County Democrats, said the fact that more Democratic ballots were pulled in this election is another indicator that officials were likely just caught off guard by the high turnout.
“I have again a lot of faith in the Jackson County Election Board and Kansas City Election Board, both the Republican and Democratic officials,” McCall said. “Especially with all of the energy surrounding stopping Amendments 4 and 5, I think that seeing those nonpartisan ballots and Democratic ballots being pulled in numbers they weren’t expecting is a sign of that kind of energy and support.”
Residents also acknowledged that the shortages were likely unintentional. But they expressed frustration that election authorities didn’t expect the higher turnout with so many important issues on the ballot.
“There was a lot of that going on with this election and so I don’t feel like even if you have statistics from previous ones that that’s necessarily going to define what is going to happen,” Knapp said.
Moving forward, she hopes to see that rectified, along with the slow response time in getting more ballots to polling places.
JCEB officials told The Beacon it has already talked about improvements. Zorich said for the next elections, they will have two electronic ADA machines at every polling location and more ballots available.
The board’s headquarters location in Independence also proved to be a challenge, Zorich said, since it’s not centrally located in the district, so it took longer than they would have liked to deliver more ballots. Spencer said they intend to learn from that experience and use it to better prepare for November.
To avoid any repeat problems, Wiley said he intends to vote earlier in the day regardless of any changes the board might make.
“I decided to wait until after work,” Wiley said. “But next time to avoid this, the earlier I get there, I shouldn’t run into that problem. … I know that that’s the best way that I can mitigate that situation.”
That’s where early voting can be useful as well, Mann said, as it allows greater flexibility for both voters and election workers. Missouri has a no-excuse absentee voting period that runs from the second Tuesday before the election to the day before the election.
“Real life happens in the middle of elections,” Mann said. “If that happens and the line is long, or you just happen to go on a busy day, you can look at that and go, ‘I can come back tomorrow,’ or two days from now, or three days from now, or even on election day in a week.”
Heading into November, McCall said he hopes that this doesn’t turn people off to the idea of voting and instead the momentum carries forward.
“I think this was just like the 100-year-flood kind of thing,” McCall said. “They really were not expecting the turnout that happened, but I would like to say let’s start to expect that turnout.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Man accused of lunging toward Ohio Democrat Amy Acton to be arraigned in Mahoning County
description: The man accused of injuring spectators at an event for Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton will go before judge Tuesday afternoon. Patrick Havas, a 38-year-old man from Canfield, faces two charges of assault and one of disorderly conduct. According to the Ohio State Highway Patrol, on Sunday, Sept. 6, troopers working as Acton’s security […]
text:
Ohio Democratic governor candidate and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, Dr. Amy Acton, looks on during a rally on April 28, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images.)The man accused of injuring spectators at an event for Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton will go before judge Tuesday afternoon. Patrick Havas, a 38-year-old man from Canfield, faces two charges of assault and one of disorderly conduct.
According to the Ohio State Highway Patrol, on Sunday, Sept. 6, troopers working as Acton’s security detail “intercepted” Havas as he forced his way through the crowd toward Acton.
“Havas knocked multiple fairgoers over while trying to get towards Dr. Acton and was found to be in possession of a taser and two pistols,” the Patrol said in a statement. “Dr. Acton was unharmed during the incident.”
Havas was then turned over to the Mahoning County Sheriff. In its statement, the Sheriff’s office noted a set of brass knuckles were recovered from Havas as well but noted “no weapons were ever brandished.” On Monday, the Sheriff asked for anyone with photos or video recordings of the incident to contact the department.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Havas is a registered voter in Mahoning County. He last voted in the 2024 general election. While the county voter file doesn’t carry a party designation for him, the last time he voted in a primary he pulled a Republican ballot for the 2016 election.
Havas is also related to Andrew Havas, a former county campaign chair for Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted’s campaign. Andrew resigned that position after NBC News reported he previously served time in jail for sexual misconduct with a minor.
Reactions
After Sunday’s incident, Acton Communications Director Addie Bullock said Dr. Acton and her husband expressed gratitude for the “swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured.”
“This kind of violence has no place in Ohio,” Bullock continued. “Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another.”
Acton’s opponents in the governor’s race were quick to condemn Havas’ actions as well.
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign stated “candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt.”
Libertarian Don Kissick said “whatever our political disagreements, violence is never an acceptable substitute for debate, elections, or the peaceful exchange of ideas.”
“Dr. Acton is my opponent in an election,” he went on, “but first and foremost she is a fellow Ohioan. I am relieved that law enforcement was there to intervene, and my thoughts are with Dr. Acton, her campaign, and everyone injured in this incident.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Gov. Mike DeWine, who helped bring Acton to statewide prominence by tapping her to lead the Department of Health, said he and his wife Fran were thankful Acton wasn’t hurt “and we send our thoughts to those who were injured.”
DeWine thanked the Highway Patrol and other law enforcement for controlling the situation and insisted “Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable.”
Attorney General Andy Wilson echoed DeWine’s praise of the patrol and stated, “political violence of any kind has no place in Ohio or our nation.”
On Monday, Acton was back on the campaign trail, taking part in Cleveland’s Labor Day Parade. She acknowledged “a rough day” in Canfield but described herself as scrappy.
“The number one thing I am fighting for is our common humanity,” Acton said. “That is what is at stake in this election. Everywhere I go, it doesn’t know party. Everyone is showing up, and they’re exhausted of the hate and the chaos and the vitriol and the purposely being pitted against one another.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Federal judge upholds Gov. Sherrill order barring ICE from some state property
description: A state executive order limiting immigration officials' access to nonpublic areas of state property does not discriminate against the feds, a judge ruled Friday.
text:
A state executive order limiting immigration officials access' to nonpublic areas of state property does not discriminate against the feds, a judge ruled Friday. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A U.S. District Court judge upheld a New Jersey executive order limiting federal immigration officials’ access to nonpublic parts of state property, ruling the federal government had failed to prove its discrimination claim.
Friday’s decision by Judge Georgette Castner keeps in place a February executive order issued by Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) that, absent judicial warrants, bars immigration officials from private parts of state land and broadly bans them from using state property as staging areas for immigration operations.
“ICE is not making New Jersey’s communities any safer. That’s why I signed an Executive Order restricting access to nonpublic state property by its untrained agents. Once again, Trump tried to stop us, and once again we won,” the governor said in a statement.
The Trump administration sued in February, arguing the executive order was preempted by federal law, impermissibly discriminated against federal immigration authorities, and unlawfully sought to regulate the federal government.
The federal statutes the Trump administration cited do not conflict with the executive order, the judge ruled, because they impose no duty to cooperate on state officials.
She added that the order does not prevent immigration enforcement, but instead bars New Jersey resources from assisting those efforts in most cases. Federal law mandating New Jersey offer its resources to aid immigration enforcement would violate the anticommandeering doctrine, which broadly says the federal government cannot dictate the content of state legislation or order state officials to enforce federal law, the judge said.
“Congress contemplated state assistance in federal immigration enforcement, but it contemplated that assistance on a voluntary basis,” wrote Castner, a Biden appointee. “The fact that New Jersey has decided not to volunteer — in the limited context of EO12 — is in accordance, not in conflict, with Congress’s design.”
Ruling the New Jersey order was preempted would improperly shift some costs for immigration enforcement onto the state, the judge ruled.
The executive order does not impermissibly regulate the federal government because it applies to state property, a distinction the judge said made New Jersey a proprietor rather than a regulator.
Even if that wasn’t the case, the order would survive because it does not “substantially interfere” with immigration enforcement as would, for example, a ban on private detention facilities that ICE uses — near exclusively —  for immigrant detention, the judge said.
“The United States does not allege facts suggesting that immigration officers ‘almost exclusively’ rely on private state-owned property to effectuate immigration enforcement or that it has to ‘entirely transform’ its approach to immigration enforcement as a result” of the executive order, the judge wrote.
The judge found the order does not discriminate against the federal government because allegations of discrimination require a showing that a policy applied unequally to similarly situated individuals or groups. Because only the federal government is tasked with civil immigration enforcement, the order does not treat federal law enforcement worse than state or local law enforcement, the judge ruled.
Spokespeople for the U.S. Department of Justice did not immediately return a request for comment. It’s unclear whether the federal government will seek to appeal the decision.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: GOP to open first-ever midterm convention in Dallas as Texas’ U.S. Senate race hangs in the balance
authors: Gabby Birenbaum, The Texas Tribune, Kayla Guo, The Texas Tribune
description: WASHINGTON — Republicans are gathering in Dallas this week for an unprecedented midterm convention, where President Donald Trump and his GOP allies will look to sell their agenda, rake in campaign cash and galvanize voters amid a difficult political climate. The convention, a two-day affair at the American Airlines Center on the edge of downtown, […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Oval Office on August 6, 2026. Trump signed an executive order during the event denying birthright citizenship to children of foreign diplomats after a loss at the U.S. Supreme Court limited an earlier order. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — Republicans are gathering in Dallas this week for an unprecedented midterm convention, where President Donald Trump and his GOP allies will look to sell their agenda, rake in campaign cash and galvanize voters amid a difficult political climate.
The convention, a two-day affair at the American Airlines Center on the edge of downtown, will put Texas at the center of the political world as the state hits the homestretch of its most competitive election cycle in years.
Texas, a longtime GOP stronghold rich with conservative donors, is a natural landing spot for the party’s first ever midterm convention. But national Republicans will also arrive at a watershed moment for the party in Texas, as Democrat James Talarico threatens to end the GOP’s three decades of statewide electoral dominance in a Senate race that most analysts see as a tossup.
While Trump has thrice carried Texas and counts many of its top politicians as allies, his approval rating in the state has sagged since his 2024 election, where he posted his best margin in Texas of his three races. Just 43% of Texas voters approved of his job performance in last month’s Texas Politics Project poll, putting him 8 points underwater in the state hosting his midterm bash.
Among Trump’s closest allies in the nation is Attorney General Ken Paxton, whom the president elevated earlier this year by endorsing him in the Republican primary runoff over Sen. John Cornyn. Paxton is now in a tight contest against Talarico, with control of the Senate — and Trump’s ability to pursue legislative accomplishments in his final two years — at stake. On the stump, Paxton frequently reminds voters of the national importance of the race, saying that if Republicans lose Texas, “we’ve lost the country.”
Control of Congress’ lower chamber could also turn on Texas — and in particular, in a handful of congressional races in the southern, heavily-Latino part of the state where Republicans redrew districts last year, at Trump’s request, to yield more GOP seats. Those races could instead deliver Democrats the U.S. House majority if the GOP fails to reverse its eroding Latino support by Election Day.
GOP path to retaining US House majority narrowing as midterms near

Republicans hope to kickstart that effort this week in Dallas, where the GOP’s top politicians will be on display with no official platform to pass or delegate votes to count — freeing them to focus on energizing their base for November.
Republicans have pitched the convention as an opportunity to do just that, with the fates of everyone from Paxton to down-ballot candidates potentially reliant on lower-propensity MAGA voters, who helped deliver the GOP a trifecta in Washington in 2024 but have proven unreliable when Trump is not on the ballot. Joe Gruters, chairman of the Republican National Committee, has described the event as a “Trumpapalooza,” making clear that candidates who show up are associated with the president.
Democrats, meanwhile, are deploying their own elected officials to Dallas for counterprogramming, and they believe the Trump-forward display could whip their own voters up into a frenzy with early voting less than six weeks away
Vice President JD Vance will deliver a keynote address on Wednesday evening, the first night of the convention, and Trump will close out the event with a speech Thursday. The rest of the schedule is devoted to highlighting the GOP’s most popular achievements from the first half of Trump’s term — much of them enacted through Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act — and emphasizing the contrast between the parties by painting Democrats as far-left extremists.
Ten Texas politicians and candidates will take the stage along with the president and Republican party leaders. The list includes Paxton, Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and Sen. Ted Cruz. Several Texas members of Congress and congressional candidates — most of them in highly competitive races — will speak as well, including three of the five nominees in seats redrawn last summer with the intention of flipping them to GOP control.
The Texas speakers include Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Flower, Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg, and candidates Carlos De La Cruz, Eric Flores and Tano Tijerina. Dallas Mayor Eric Johnson will also address the convention.
In an interview on Patrick’s podcast last week, Trump said he wanted to recreate the same energy generated by conventions in presidential election years.
“The conventions have been great, and a lot of good things happen,” Trump said. “And it brings unity.”
The president will arrive in Dallas amid intense interest in his plans for the Senate race in Texas, where Talarico has built a narrow polling lead and vastly outspent Paxton. Trump’s super PAC coffers, brimming with more than $400 million, are highly coveted by a number of campaigns in Texas and elsewhere, including other Senate battlegrounds where advertising dollars go much further. Trump’s political team made its first general election ad buy on Saturday in Texas — to the tune of $10 million for streaming and digital ads boosting Paxton and attacking Talarico — emphasizing the centrality of the Lone Star State to the president’s plans this cycle.
Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms

Trump said last week that he has close to $1 billion available for political spending, and that he plans to use up to $500 million in the midterms.
The president has said he’s committed to helping Paxton campaign while also disparaging his appearance on multiple occasions last week. At one point, the president said that while “you might not like the way he dresses” or “the way he looks,” Paxton has been the best attorney general in the country.
“We’re going to have a lot of speakers,” Trump told Patrick of the convention. “And the ones we want to focus on will be, obviously, Ken Paxton. We got to get him elected. He’s a good man. I know him very well. He really was a great attorney general.”
The Republican National Committee is aiming to feature a mix of GOP candidates and everyday Americans to promote an array of policy wins and aspirations. Topics on the menu include the implementation of the “no tax on tips” policy, which allows workers to claim a deduction on tip income, and the creation of Trump Accounts, investment vehicles for kids. Both were priorities of Cruz that made it into the One Big Beautiful Bill.
Each hour of the convention will be themed with different elements of the GOP agenda, including tax cuts, border enforcement and “cultural common sense.” Candidates in target districts will be showcased on both nights, and Texas politicians and candidates are expected to be featured.
One way Republicans hope to get the base fired up in a tough cycle? Bash the opposition.
The convention schedule will feature video presentations drawing a contrast with Democratic candidates in marquee races. The event will feature video spots of Democrats saying things the GOP has spent the midterm cycle casting as radical and disqualifying. It is expected to include ample clips of Talarico, according to a person familiar with Republicans’ midterm planning.
Rep. Roger Williams, R-Willow Park, said the contrast will be stark.
“All of us are going to get the message out,” Williams said. “It really has great timing from our standpoint, because now we can compare socialism, Marxism, communism with what Texas values are all about and American values: capitalism and free markets.”
Many GOP elected officials’ participation in the convention has been up in the air, with dozens of U.S. House members skipping out or still deciding. But participation among Texas’ elected officials figures to be strong.
In brief interviews, a majority of Texas’ Republican delegation surveyed in Washington said they planned to attend.
“We’re Texas — so we kind of better be there,” said Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Tyler, who said he will be in Dallas for the festivities.
The convention also represents a fundraising opportunity for Republicans across the country to tap Dallas’ deep donor pool.
Trump highlighted Dallas Mavericks owner Miriam Adelson, who gave over $100 million to Trump’s reelection effort in 2024, in his conversation with Patrick.
“We’re having it in Dallas,” Trump said. “We have it in the great basketball arena, and Miriam has been fantastic. She’s the owner of the team. She’s been really great. And it’s going to be a phenomenal two days.”
But some Republicans are passing based on the minimum $25,000 the National Republican Congressional Committee is reportedly asking each House GOP member to pony up if they want to attend.
Rep. Beth Van Duyne, R-Irving, defended the cost in an interview with TMZ.
“Part of our dues are to make sure that we’re supporting other candidates who are in very tough, competitive races around the country,” Van Duyne said. “I think what that was is just kind of an incentive that we need to make sure that we’re all supporting our party.”
Shoffner, Cotton win primaries for U.S. Senate seat in Arkansas

The path to House and Senate majorities could very well run through Texas this cycle, with Republicans holding a razor-thin margin in the House and Democrats looking to pick up four spots in the Senate while defending their current seats.
Texas Republicans gerrymandered the state’s congressional lines last year at Trump’s behest, shading five districts a darker red to help pad their House majority. But with persistent backlash to high costs and the Trump administration’s war in Iran and aggressive deportation campaign — and Latino voters appearing to turn on the GOP — competitive polling in some South Texas districts has raised the specter of a “dummymander,” in which the aggressive redraw backfires on Republicans.
Texas Democrats, meanwhile, plan to hold two news conferences a day near the convention grounds, where their own national and state officials will be featured.
Talarico plans to host a “Love Thy Neighbor” grocery drive beginning Wednesday, dubbing the Republican convention a “Billionaire Ball celebrating corrupt tariffs, billionaire tax breaks and a new forever war that are all driving grocery costs through the roof.”
“Billionaire mega-donors and their puppet politicians will gather at a convention in Dallas to clink champagne glasses and toast their own corruption,” Talarico said in a statement last week. “We’ll be doing something different.”
This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: How Gloria Steinem and bell hooks created the feminism that shaped my life
description: I can’t really remember the exact moment I began identifying as a feminist. I know it was early on – before I even knew what the word meant, before my first date, before someone told me I had to wear a bra, before the first time a man made me feel inferior. Somewhere between Claire […]
text:
Gloria Steinem, Mae Suramek, and bell hooks during one of Steinem's visits to Berea. Steinem and hooks were friends and collaborators. (Photo provided)I can’t really remember the exact moment I began identifying as a feminist. I know it was early on – before I even knew what the word meant, before my first date, before someone told me I had to wear a bra, before the first time a man made me feel inferior. Somewhere between Claire Huxtable practicing law while simultaneously raising five children, Diana Prince wielding her magic lasso, and me rolling up my Barbie’s sleeves to rescue entire fictional villages from deadly quick sand, an undeniable forbidden power began to bubble deep down inside me.  And yes, it felt forbidden during the latter part of the 80’s when nurses still wore crisp white uniformed dresses and flight attendants were called air hostesses. I felt, even as a 13-year-old girl, the quiet but deadly suffocation of societal norms and expectations crushing down on me. 
And this is how I found myself with my first copy of Ms. magazine 40 years ago. Gloria Steinem’s glorious brainchild to bring feminism to the masses and to provide more than anything – validation that the forbidden power bubbling inside of me, wasn’t forbidden at all. In fact women all over the world possessed it too – even if they didn’t know it yet. Ms. magazine was like a secret little members-only club I could retreat to monthly where I didn’t have to smile on demand or get out of the way for men.
Gloria, who died last week, and Ms. would carry me well through high school and college, into young adulthood when that bubbling forbidden power, like a tea kettle that had been slowly percolating for years, grew from a soft whistle into a loud unrelenting siren of second wave feminism. There was nothing forbidden about my power in my early 20s – it became unapologetic, fearless, and defiant. I saw so clearly the inequities women faced in the workplace, the systemic discrimination against women in housing, and good Lord – the violence, the sanctioned and systemic violence in every magazine ad, every college campus, every dark alleyway, and every board room. It was so overpowering, so devastating I would spend the bulk of my professional life trying my darndest to dismantle it by working in domestic violence shelters, rape crisis centers, and human rights organizations.
And if Gloria’s second wave feminism rose to a screeching teapot crescendo in my young adulthood, the feminism of her good friend, bell hooks exploded and blew the entire pot off the stove in my 30s. It became undeniable, indisputable that sexism and racism were so deeply connected and had to be dismantled together. And that voices and perspectives of women of color were often missing in the very movement that I thought I was a part of all along. 
The late bell hooks joined the faculty of my alma mater, Berea College the same year I returned to work at Berea as alumni director and to have her voice so close, her presence surrounding me daily, was a gift that was life-changing in a way that I don’t think I recognized at the time. bell imparted so much wisdom on me during the 15 or so years that I knew her, but the funny thing is that I had no idea she was doing it at the time. 
When she first met my white husband and embraced him fully, trusting my judgment in choosing him as a partner, seeing him as someone who “divested of male privilege, embraced feminist politics, and is a worthy comrade in struggle.” It didn’t occur to me why she was so accepting of him until I read these words she wrote in her book “Feminism is for Everybody” many years later.  
Three months after I gave birth, when she showed up at my door with a bag of baby clothes she had hand selected from our local Goodwill, honoring my role as a mother of a boy and my responsibility to raise him not to seek domination. When I became executive director of our regional rape crisis center, and she invited herself to join our staff retreat and spent six hours grounding 17 women, pouring gratitude and love into the therapists and advocates, acknowledging the impact of secondary trauma, and helping us understand the systemic reality of how white supremacist capitalist patriarchy fuels violence against women. 
When she invited me back as a speaker at the bell hooks Institute at a time in my life I no longer worked in “the movement” and had left the advocacy world to open a restaurant. I tried to decline, but she wouldn’t let me, firmly insisting that love and community were essential in dismantling systems of oppression. bell’s combination of radical love, community, intersectionality, and revolutionary feminism finally gave me – a brown daughter of immigrants living in Kentucky – a place in feminism. And she somehow managed to offer this priceless gift to me without a single lecture or book. 
To the rest of the world, Gloria Steinem and bell hooks were feminist icons who will be documented and studied in history books, and whose unwavering legacies will continue to challenge systems of domination and oppression. To me, Gloria and bell made feminism accessible. Beyond feminist theory, academic publications, and public discourse, they gave 13-year old me permission to finally own my power, and 30-year old me the courage to to do something worthwhile with it.

title: National grant will expand free arts classes for older Delawareans
description: A $77,500 award will help Access Creative Aging reach 480 participants at libraries and senior centers through June 2028 DOVER, Del. — Hundreds of older Delawareans will gain access to free arts classes through a $77,500 national grant awarded to the Delaware Division of the Arts. The funding will expand Access Creative Aging, a statewide program offering ad[...]
text:
Photo: Image provided by the Delaware Division of the Arts
A $77,500 award will help Access Creative Aging reach 480 participants at libraries and senior centers through June 2028
DOVER, Del. — Hundreds of older Delawareans will gain access to free arts classes through a $77,500 national grant awarded to the Delaware Division of the Arts.
The funding will expand Access Creative Aging, a statewide program offering adults ages 55 and older free, eight-week workshops in pottery, poetry, painting, dance, theater, jewelry design and other creative disciplines.
Over two grant cycles running through June 2028, the division plans to reach 480 participants at 20 public libraries and 12 senior centers. The expansion is expected to provide more than 640 hours of instruction across all three counties.
“The arts are a proven tool for keeping older Delawareans healthy, connected and engaged,” Gov. Matt Meyer said. “This funding will ensure Delaware continues to lead, allowing us to reach hundreds more seniors who deserve access to these programs.”
From pilot program to statewide initiative
The Delaware Division of the Arts launched Access Creative Aging in 2022 as a pilot program at eight public libraries. The initiative has since grown into a central part of the division’s Arts and Community programming.
The program has served more than 400 older adults and delivered more than 520 hours of free instruction. Classes are led by trained teaching artists at libraries and senior centers.
The program is administered in partnership with the Delaware Division of Libraries and the Division of Services for Aging and Adults with Physical Disabilities.
Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez said cooperation among the agencies helped transform the initial library pilot into a statewide program.
“That partnership is what turned a pilot program in eight libraries into a statewide model for how the arts support healthy aging,” Patibanda-Sanchez said. “This award reflects the power of state agencies working together and our commitment to making sure that work reaches every Delawarean, regardless of income or geography.”
Classes build confidence and connections
A study conducted during the program’s first year found that 92% of participants reported increased confidence in their ability to learn new skills. Fifty-six percent said their confidence increased significantly.
The study also found that 96% of participants reported an improved sense of accomplishment and mastery. No participants reported a decline in either measure.
More recent surveys found that participants formed friendships, continued practicing their chosen art forms after their classes ended and developed a stronger sense of belonging.
“Having little to no disposable income, the free classes are a true godsend,” one participant wrote.
Another participant said the program encouraged continued learning and experimentation.
“I feel more confident about making creative decisions and experimenting than I did before,” the participant wrote. “I have invested funds to purchase additional materials and supplies and have started working on my own projects.”
Demand exceeds available space
Jessica Ball, director of the Delaware Division of the Arts, said demand for the classes has consistently exceeded the program’s capacity.
“Delaware’s older adult population is growing rapidly, and demand for Access Creative Aging programming has consistently outpaced our capacity,” Ball said. “This award will allow us to bring high-quality, free arts programming to more Delawareans in more communities, including those with the least access to the arts.”
State officials said Delaware’s population of adults ages 55 and older is projected to grow by more than 50% by 2030.
The new funding will support additional workshops, the training of new teaching artists and expanded access through libraries and senior services organizations.
Delaware is one of 28 state and jurisdictional arts agencies receiving grants through Creative Aging, Creative Futures, a partnership between the National Assembly of State Arts Agencies and E.A. Michelson Philanthropy. The initiative awarded more than $2.2 million nationally to promote learning, creativity, well-being and social engagement among older adults.
The national program builds on two earlier initiatives focused on helping state arts agencies expand services for older residents and integrate arts programming into aging services.
To Go Box



What: Access Creative Aging
Who: Delaware residents ages 55 and older
Programs: Free, eight-week workshops in painting, pottery, poetry, dance, theater, jewelry design and other art forms
Locations: Participating public libraries and senior centers throughout Delaware
Expansion goal: 480 participants at 20 libraries and 12 senior centers through June 2028
Learn more: Visit https://arts.delaware.gov/programs-events/delaware-creative-aging/

title: As extreme weather worsens, Black and Hispanic homeowners are paying more for insurance
description: This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here. Homeowners in Hispanic and Black communities nationwide are paying a disproportionate share of skyrocketing home insurance costs, according to a recent report. The disparities[...]
text:
House mortgage real estate money dollar home insurance. Getty ImagesThis article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
Homeowners in Hispanic and Black communities nationwide are paying a disproportionate share of skyrocketing home insurance costs, according to a recent report. The disparities leave communities of color at greater risk as climate change increases the frequency of billion-dollar disasters.
The report, released in July by the Consumer Federation of America, a nonprofit representing nearly 250 consumer groups, concluded that homeowners in predominantly Hispanic ZIP codes pay on average a 30 percent higher premium ($950 more annually) compared with homeowners in white communities. In predominantly Black ZIP codes, homeowners pay, on average, a 16 percent higher premium ($500 more annually).
The findings were based on an analysis of identical policies across communities, eliminating the possibility the inequities were related to differences among homeowners, their homes or what they chose to insure, the report said. Local risk factors could be responsible for some of the disparities, although even when such factors were accounted for the gap remained large.
“We’ve talked a lot about our insurance affordability crisis,” said Sharon Cornelissen, director of housing at the Consumer Federation of America and a co-author of the report. “What we haven’t really talked about is sort of the racially inequitable impacts of that, and that Black and Hispanic homeowners are particularly struggling.”
The inequities add up to at least $28,500 in additional insurance costs over the span of a 30-year mortgage for homeowners in Hispanic communities and $15,000 for homeowners in Black communities, according to the report. The situation points to a legacy of redlining in home insurance that continues to challenge communities of color when it comes to homeownership and exposure to risk, although the discrimination today may be inadvertent.
The historical practice of redlining involved the designation of certain neighborhoods as “hazardous” for mortgage lending, based largely on the race of residents. People in these neighborhoods were denied home loans, leading to lower home values and less homeownership. Although redlining ended in 1968 with the Fair Housing Act, the practice has left a legacy of segregation and disparities in these neighborhoods that endures today when it comes to health care, education, incarceration, access to nutritious food and public investment in infrastructure. The inequities also have left these communities more vulnerable to climate impacts such as heat.
Mark Friedlander, spokesman for the Insurance Information Institute, an industry group, said premiums are based on risk and not race or ethnicity and that the system used to establish premiums is actuarially grounded and heavily regulated.
“Using race, or any proxy for race, to set insurance rates is illegal in every U.S. jurisdiction, and state insurance regulators review and approve the rating factors insurers use precisely to guard against that,” he said in a statement provided to Inside Climate News. “Many of the communities cited in reports like this are located in areas with objectively higher catastrophe exposure or higher costs to rebuild and repair after a loss.”
The report found the most acute home insurance disparity among homeowners in predominantly Hispanic ZIP codes in Florida, where they pay on average 58 percent more ($5,014 annually) for the same coverage as those in white communities. In the next four states, the gap was pronounced, but smaller: 20 percent ($431) in New York, 18 percent ($278) in Washington, 16 percent ($244) in Massachusetts and 15 percent ($633) in Kansas.
The inequities in Florida, where homeowners have been particularly hard-hit by insurance costs, represent “an enormous amount of money,” said Moira Birss, senior fellow at the Climate and Community Institute, a progressive think tank. “And so when we’re thinking about how we’re having an affordability crisis in this country … that’s unconscionable.”
When it comes to predominantly Black ZIP codes, the inequities are greatest in Michigan at 74 percent ($1,768 annually), followed by Pennsylvania at 57 percent ($1,048), New Jersey at 22 percent ($332), Massachusetts at 20 percent ($321) and New York at 19 percent ($417).
Meanwhile, the cost of insurance for the typical homeowner jumped by 24 percent between 2021 and 2024, according to the report, based on previous research by the Consumer Federation of America. Greenhouse gas emissions, primarily those associated with fossil fuels, are heating the global climate, shifting weather patterns and leading to more extreme disasters such as hurricanes and wildfires. That risk is moving insurance companies to raise rates.
Insurance companies have provided fewer and more expensive options in communities of color compared with white communities, the report said. It highlighted a $17.5 million settlement from the 1990s over a lawsuit alleging the insurance company Nationwide discouraged agents from selling coverage in Black neighborhoods, labeled Black ZIP codes as undesirable and used racial profiling to deny insurance to Black homeowners. American Family Mutual Insurance Company similarly agreed to pay more than $16 million in a settlement to Black homeowners who were provided inferior policies and, in some cases, denied coverage based on race.
More recently insurers have adopted new proprietary methods for determining premiums and claims payments, including some incorporating artificial intelligence, that raise concerns about possible discrimination, according to the report. For instance, previous research by the Consumer Federation of America found that homeowners with lower credit scores pay an average penalty of $1,996 annually, or 99 percent more, for insurance, a concern considering longstanding structural factors that have meant communities of color tend to have lower credit scores.
“I’m not saying that they have some secret race factor that they put into their model,” Cornelissen said. “A lot of this bias can kind of creep in if they’re not paying attention to potential unequal impacts. A lot of this could be through AI models or other factors that have a disproportionate impact on Black and Hispanic communities.”
Friedlander said the best way to make insurance more affordable and equitable is by reducing risk through resilience efforts such as strengthening building codes and increasing mitigation funding.
The report called on states to enforce fair housing laws and demand more transparency and accountability.
“Unless the insurance industry wants to give us more information about why this is happening,” Birss said, “it’s pretty hard not to interpret this as pretty serious racial discrimination.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: A California cloud-seeding company created rain near Homer — and an uproar
description: This story was originally published by the Anchorage Press.  A California tech company is facing an uproar from local residents and elected officials after launching a drone near the small Alaska fishing town of Homer with a goal fit for a sci-fi novel: to create rain and snow. The company, Rainmaker Technology Corp., says it […]
text:
A California tech company recently tested its drone-based cloud-seeding technology in Alaska. (Photo courtesy of Rainmaker Technology Corp.) This story was originally published by the Anchorage Press. 
A California tech company is facing an uproar from local residents and elected officials after launching a drone near the small Alaska fishing town of Homer with a goal fit for a sci-fi novel: to create rain and snow.
The company, Rainmaker Technology Corp., says it produced 19 million gallons of water in the sky near Homer in about three hours Aug. 23 by dispersing a small amount of silver iodide — a chemical that induces precipitation under the right atmospheric conditions — from a drone.
It was a training run for a company whose mission is to alleviate water scarcity in drought-stricken areas and ultimately to make the planet more habitable as it warms.
Rainmaker says it received the necessary regulatory approvals and notified state officials before launching its operation. But local representatives say they learned about the test after the fact — and that many of their constituents, even those typically divided over politics, are united in concern.
“The fact that these guys are literally dropping materials on constituents without any notification or checklist of what should occur prior to the flight is clearly a gap in responsible lawmaking,” said Peter Micciche, the mayor of the Kenai Peninsula Borough.
The issue has generated one of the largest outpourings of local opposition “in a very, very long time,” said state Rep. Sarah Vance, a Republican who represents Homer and its surroundings.
Vance sent a letter this week to Rainmaker asking it to “cease and desist” its operations in her district. She also asked that the company hold a public open house.
Rainmaker mainly operates in the Lower 48, where it’s trying to revive Utah’s Great Salt Lake, save the Colorado River and help snow-starved ski resorts stay in business. Its work is known as cloud seeding, one of several technologies that startups are promoting as scientists and investors look for ways to blunt the impacts of global climate change.
The company came to Alaska just to test its process, which works only when clouds are cold enough for ice to form around the silver iodide particles, according to the company’s chief executive, Augustus Doricko.     
Augustus Doricko, 26, is chief executive of Rainmaker Technology Corp. (Photo courtesy of Rainmaker)

But cloud seeding also has potential uses — enhancing hydropower and protecting glaciers — that are “immediately relevant to Alaska,” said Doricko, 26.
The company launched a drone from two sites near the head of Kachemak Bay, some 20 miles northeast of Homer.
The drone was about the size of a lawn mower, Doricko said. It held several small flares. Once it reached a certain elevation — thousands of feet in the air, in the middle of a supercool cloud — the flares combusted and released silver iodide dust into the air, Doricko said.
In total, the company dispersed some 375 grams of silver iodide — a little less than a pound — over a wide area, according to a technical corporate report. Doricko asserted that the chemical is totally safe at those levels; the resulting increase in silver concentrations on the ground is orders of magnitude less than the 100 parts per billion threshold set by the Environmental Protection Agency for drinking water, he said.
“In a certain sense, I am running a conservation company, or at least a company that’s trying to make our ecosystems and our farms healthier, and more green,” Doricko said. “So, it would be pretty ridiculous if I was using something that acted to the contrary of that.”
Micciche, the mayor, said he’s not especially concerned about silver iodide.
“But the fact that someone can drop something from a drone on my constituency without any prior notification or public comment, in my view, is inadequate,” he said.
“The contrail people are saying, ‘See, I told you so.’ But it’s the other 85% of the population that’s like, ‘Wait a minute, I can’t drop things on my neighbors without public notice… or some sort of permit,’” Micciche added.
Micciche said he plans to introduce a resolution and ordinance at the next borough assembly meeting, with the intent to increase local oversight over cloud-seeding.
The issue has struck a chord not only in conservative circles and among politicians like Micciche and Vance, but also among local environmental advocates.
Cooper Freeman, a Homer resident and Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, a national conservation group, said he has concerns, too.
“At best, it’s absolutely bizarre,” Freeman said in a text message. “At worst, it’s a dangerous and potentially toxic false solution to addressing the severe climate disruption facing the state.”
Meanwhile, Vance, the state legislator, said she is pushing Rainmaker for an open house so they can explain their technology and hear directly from the public.
She said her constituents “don’t want weather modification over our skies or in our skies.”
Doricko said he understands the concerns.
“I’m really empathetic to people that have questions about what we’re doing, right? You hear about a tech company with a mulleted CEO that’s in his 20s, that’s modifying the weather. That should absolutely raise eyebrows,” he said.
But Doricko added that companies have tested cloud-seeding technology for decades— though experts also have long questioned its effectiveness. And he said that even though 19 million gallons of water sounds like a lot — and could provide drinking water to more than 150 households for a year — it’s not enough to create a “torrential downpour” or blizzard. That amount equates to about 0.01 of an inch of rain across 100 square miles.
Rainmaker is not planning another test in Alaska next summer, Doricko added. But the company is working to schedule a town hall.
“We absolutely have to talk to the folks before we operate, and we did, and we got those approvals,” he said.
He said Rainmaker notified the Alaska Department of Natural Resources and reached out to the region’s Alaska Native corporation and a local tribal government. The company also received approvals from the Federal Aviation Administration.
A document that Rainmaker says it presented to state land managers — and that the company shared with the Anchorage Press — describes plans to “conduct atmospheric data collection, cloud seeding feasibility assessments, and precipitation enhancement research via Aerosol Dispersal System (ADS) and silver iodide (AgI) flare dispersal at altitude.”
After meeting with company representatives, the Alaska Department of Natural Resources issued a letter to Rainmaker noting that the use of a drone for research is a generally allowed use on state land, meaning it does not require a permit.
The agency does not have jurisdiction over cloud-seeding, and did not issue any specific authorization for it, according to spokesperson Lorraine Henry.
Another state regulatory agency, the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation, “is aware of Rainmaker’s reported activity and is reviewing the available information in coordination with other state agencies,” Sam Dapcevich, an agency spokesperson, said in an email.
“A more thorough response with our evaluation will follow in the coming days,” he added.
Doricko, for his part, said he’s “absolutely down” to do more outreach in the future.
He just insisted on one thing for the town hall: metal detectors at the door.
This story was originally published by Anchorage Press, the revived independent alt-weekly. Find a place to pick up a copy of their first print issue on this map.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Federal appeals court to consider Louisiana’s arguments for banning telehealth abortion
description: The U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals will consider Louisiana’s arguments for tightening federal policy around a common abortion and miscarriage drug.
text:
The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will hear oral arguments for Louisiana v. U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday at the federal courthouse in New Orleans. Medication abortion has become the most common form of abortion since Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022, and telehealth prescriptions have continued to rise. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)This week, the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals will consider Louisiana’s arguments for tightening federal policy around a common abortion and miscarriage drug. The primary target of Louisiana v. Food and Drug Administration and similar lawsuits against mifepristone is to end a Biden-era policy allowing abortion pills to be prescribed without an in-person visit with a provider.
Medication abortion has become the most common form of abortion since Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022, and telehealth prescriptions have continued to rise. The Biden administration loosened telehealth regulations in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
According to the Guttmacher Institute, a research think tank that supports abortion access, about 91,000 abortions were provided last year via telehealth prescription of abortion medication sent by mail to states with bans, including more than 9,300 in Louisiana.
The FDA’s policy that mailing abortion pills is safe is unlikely to change in the next few months. The Trump administration has asked courts to delay the cases until it finishes a highly anticipated safety review about mifepristone. Numerous studies have concluded the medicine, which also is used to manage miscarriage treatment, is safe to prescribe through telehealth.
The case is one of three federal lawsuits — the others are being considered in Missouri and Texas — that could affect telehealth access to mifepristone nationwide.
“What this is doing is shutting down access to people in states that have committed to continuing to make abortion legal, and it will impact people in all 50 states,” said Melissa Grant, co-founder of carafem, which operates telehealth or physical health centers in 21 states where abortion remains legal.
Earlier this year, the 5th Circuit ruled in favor of Louisiana’s motion to temporarily reinstate an old rule that patients could only receive mifepristone in person. The Supreme Court blocked that ruling, allowing telehealth abortion to continue as the case progresses. Whatever the appeals court rules this time, it will likely go back to the Supreme Court for a final ruling on Louisiana’s motion to reverse the policy until the case is decided on the merits.
Two years ago, the U.S. Supreme Court dismissed a lawsuit seeking to restrict mifepristone, brought by Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, ruling the doctor-plaintiffs did not have proper standing to sue.
But Gabriella McIntyre, legal counsel of Alliance Defending Freedom, which is helping to defend Louisiana and one of its residents, a co-plaintiff who says her then-boyfriend coerced her into taking abortion pills, believes her team can persuade the 5th Circuit on Wednesday that Louisiana has proper standing.



Quotation







If Louisiana wins this case, we’re going to see for the first time what it looks like under an actual Dobbs regime, where pro-life states get to enforce their laws protecting the unborn.


– Gabriella McIntyre, legal counsel of Alliance Defending Freedom


The state is arguing in part that the 2023 FDA rule violated the 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision by allowing for telehealth abortion and abortion by mail in states that banned abortion, like Louisiana. The FDA has so far argued Louisiana doesn’t have standing to sue and that it needs more time to review the drug’s safety. Two mifepristone drugmakers have intervened on the FDA’s side.
“If Louisiana wins this case, we’re going to see for the first time what it looks like under an actual Dobbs regime, where pro-life states get to enforce their laws protecting the unborn,” McIntyre said.
Abortion law expert Mary Ziegler said she expects the conservative 5th Circuit to side with Louisiana and that its justification will likely serve as a roadmap for the U.S. Supreme Court.
“The 5th Circuit, they’re going to be writing almost like a proposed first draft for the U.S. Supreme Court,” Ziegler said. “Maybe the court has questions about standing again so, ‘We want to focus the hearing and the opinions on standing because we think that’s the hurdle that we have to overcome to get the five votes at the Supreme Court.’ Or do they talk about everything, and just sort of let the chips fall where they may?”
The Trump administration has reversed several Biden-era reproductive health policies, but not the 2023 rule, citing an ongoing review expected to be released after the November midterm elections. But recently confirmed Attorney General Todd Blanche recently promised faith leaders he will focus on restricting abortion pill access.
Oral arguments will be livestreamed through the court system at 9 a.m. CDT on Wednesday.



South Carolina supports Louisiana efforts
In February, South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson joined more than 20 other states in supporting Louisiana in its case.
“This is about protecting life, but it’s also about state sovereignty,” Wilson said in a statement at the time. “What good does it do for one state to pass a law banning something, like chemical abortion drugs, if another state is still allowed to mail them into our state?”
Then in May, the states unsuccessfully asked the Supreme Court to uphold a ruling from the New Orleans-based, U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals, which would have banned mifepristone from being mailed. The ruling would have applied to the whole country, not just Louisiana.
“As Attorney General, I have supported reforms at the state and federal level to reclassify mifepristone and outlaw telehealth abortions,” Wilson said at the time.
“This rule has wide-ranging and dangerous effects on citizens in every state,” Wilson added. “Doctors in other states should not be able to circumvent our state law by shipping mifepristone across state lines.”



Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.
