name: Florida Phoenix
title: Hit dogs holler over Hope Florida disclosure
description: Just when you thought state politics could not possibly get sleazier, Hope Florida comes roaring back from the dead, putrid yet powerful, casting a light on the breathtaking arrogance and corruption of Florida’s government. Gov. Ron DeSantis, Attorney General James Uthmeier, and U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody thought they’d killed it and driven a stake through […]
text:
Casey and Ron DeSantis in Tampa on May 20, 2025. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Just when you thought state politics could not possibly get sleazier, Hope Florida comes roaring back from the dead, putrid yet powerful, casting a light on the breathtaking arrogance and corruption of Florida’s government.
Gov. Ron DeSantis, Attorney General James Uthmeier, and U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody thought they’d killed it and driven a stake through its dirty little heart.
A Leon County grand jury looked into the scandal. But, since they could not get the people involved to tell the truth about how and by whom $10 million of taxpayer money disappeared into political causes, they could not bring charges.
DeSantis, Uthmeier, and Moody counted on that report never seeing the light of day.
But, as is the way with explosive secret reports, it was leaked.
To a reporter.
God forbid the public learn what politicians and their enablers do with public money.
The parties did not express concern, much less remorse.
They attacked journalists.
During a press conference, Uthmeier threatened to bring criminal charges when asked about the matter: “Are you trying to solicit a crime here in violation of the law?”
Somewhat unconvincingly, he went on, insisting, “Nobody did anything wrong here; there was not even probable cause to move forward. This is a hoax.”
Which are you going to believe, Florida’s law-challenged AG or your lying eyes?
DeSantis agreed: “The only crime that was apparent was whoever leaked the grand jury report.”
You may recall First Lady Casey DeSantis founded Hope Florida in 2021, claiming it was a community support program to connect people with faith-based or other non-government assistance. She called it “a philosophy.”
Two years later, the Hope Florida Foundation appeared, its stated purpose to support the Department of Children and Families.
 The money
It’s a 501(c)(3), the kind of nonprofit that must, by law, follow strict limits on political involvement and lobbying.
It soon became clear there was shady stuff going on. DCF failed to make public Hope Florida Foundation’s fiscal plan, code of ethics, tax documents, and results, as required by law.
Then a Medicaid contractor that had over-billed the state had to cough up a $67 million settlement, supposedly repaying the taxpayers.
Of that money, $10 million was (strangely) “donated” to the Hope Florida Foundation.
That $10 million (very strangely) ended up in a couple of political action committees controlled by Ron DeSantis’s chief of staff, a fellow by the name of James Uthmeier.
The money got fed back into the state Republican Party machine to fuel its fight against a constitutional amendment to legalize recreational marijuana.
Uthmeier’s PAC was called Keep Florida Clean.
(You can’t make this stuff up).
Many in the Florida Legislature were, to put it mildly, unimpressed.
Then-House Speaker Daniel Perez said the Hope Florida business looked “as though it could be illegal.”
Rep. Alex Andrade, chair of the House Healthcare subcommittee, suggested fraud might be involved and the Hope Florida “donation” could be “money laundering.”
Ron DeSantis flapped his wings like an outraged hen and squawked that these “jackasses” were merely trying to “smear” his wife and crush her dreams of political advancement.
At the time, Casey DeSantis seemed to be considering a run to succeed her husband as governor.
Andrade launched an investigation.
Then ended it. Almost no one involved would talk.
 ‘Mistakes were made’
He did get Joshua Hay, then chairman of the Hope Florida Foundation board, to testify under oath, but didn’t get much out of it — other than that Hay seemed spectacularly ignorant of what goes on in the charity he runs.
“I cannot confirm what the funds were used for,” Hay said. “We have no monitoring procedures.”
He added, “Mistakes were made.”
State Attorney Jack Campbell in Leon County agreed mistakes had, indeed, been made. He convened a grand jury to discover who made them.
What the grand jury unearthed is pretty damning, finding the Hope Florida Foundation “misappropriated” taxpayer money as “part of a sophisticated scheme.”
The report said, “While we can’t prove who is responsible, we can plainly see that taxpayer money was misused for political purposes.”
It also states: “Nobody will take responsibility for deciding the $10 million of taxpayer money would go to Hope Florida.”
“This decision was the original misappropriation, and no witness would take responsibility for making the decision or had any memory of who made it.”
Those in charge of running this dubious show insist they acted on legal advice. So, it was all fine.
Besides, they couldn’t remember what happened.
It’s a mystery!
Those who should have known better turned a blind eye. The report said Ashley Moody’s chief deputy failed to conduct “due diligence to ensure the proper appropriation of taxpayer funds.”
Those most deeply implicated now go around pitching loud hissy fits.
Uthmeier yelped the whole thing was nothing more than a “politically motivated witch hunt driven by the Democrats and a far left Democrat state attorney.”
Sounds a little desperate: Those of us in North Florida know Jack Campbell is about as “far left” as a ham sandwich.
 Indignance
As for the people at the top of the power pile getting all red-faced and indignant over the grand jury report, well, as we say here in “far left” Tallahassee, a hit dog will holler.
Meanwhile in the blue corner, the Florida Democratic Party can’t believe its luck: The midterms are coming and the Republicans are trying to excuse the inexcusable.
Angie Nixon says Ashley Moody, her opponent in the 2026 Senate race, should resign.
José Javier Rodriguez, who’s running against Uthmeier for attorney general, calls the Hope Florida mess “the most brazen act of political corruption we have seen here in Florida.”
“My opponent is a criminal,” he says.
Gubernatorial candidate David Jolly doesn’t want Casey DeSantis attacked over Hope Florida: “I think she was used.”
Very gentlemanly.
But he’s not going to ignore the issue: “The scheme de-funded healthcare services for poor children to instead advance the political agenda of Gov. Ron DeSantis.”
Jolly and the rest of the Dems are getting some help from Florida Republicans, too.
GOP nominee Byron Donalds, forced to answer questions about the grand jury report at every campaign stop, insists voters aren’t that interested.
Come on, can’t we please talk about something else?
But even some Republicans, especially those Ron DeSantis has antagonized, aren’t inclined to talk about something else.
Sen. Rick Scott, no fan of Florida’s current governor, demands “accountability.” Scott’s company defrauded Medicare of $1.7 billion. Nevertheless, he’s getting pious on Hope Florida’s dodgy finances: “Money designated to help poor kids was diverted to political ads.”
 ‘Disgrace’
Don Gaetz, a longtime state senator, says Hope Florida “brings disgrace onto the Florida government.”
He’s pushing “a bipartisan coalition that simply makes sure this doesn’t happen again.”
Not a good look for the Rs less than two months before an election.
Of course, Democrats shouldn’t get giddy: Polls in the races for governor, U.S. senator, and state attorney general still favor Republicans, although they’ve been tightening up: Jolly is within a few points of Donalds, even leading in some polls.
But political scandals have a way of hanging around. They show up in campaign commercials, further souring the mood of voters sick of high gas prices, grocery store sticker shock, the Iran war, Uthmeier’s inflated adjunct professor salary (plus his arrogance), and Ron DeSantis’ attacks on education (plus his arrogance), not to mention Florida’s sky-high rents and unaffordable insurance.
Will Hope Florida make a difference? Maybe we’ll find out in November.
Maybe a couple of long-shot Democrats will break through.
What is certain is that the Hope Florida “philosophy” is as dead as a door nail.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Help preserve the Preserve in Old Saybrook
description: Logging the Preserve threatens one of a few remaining mature coastal forests -- one that took shape long before our ancestors arrived.
text:
As you enter The Preserve in Old Saybrook, stop and look up. A cool, moist air escapes the forest and lightly touches your face. With feet firmly planted, close your eyes and take in a deep breath. Your lungs fill with fresh, oxygen rich air, emanating from millions of respiring oak leaves. Their motto: carbon in, oxygen out. Just what we humans need for a livable planet.
Now, with every cell in your body energized, step on in.

Sierra Ferris

Moving along a winding path, shaded by a grand old tree canopy, listen to birds singing their happy songs. Neuroscience tells us bird song, or simply walking in a forest, calms the senses and elevates the mood. It’s a nice break from our hectic days.
As you meander, watch closely. Squirrels forage and watch you pass by from the limbs above. And if you’re lucky, you catch a glimpse of a chipmunk, scurrying under and across downed tree trunks, sharply chirping to his or her community, that visitors have arrived. Trees are their home, whether standing tall or sprawled across the forest floor.
Look closer still into the dense understory. Mushrooms, moss, and ferns grow in abundance, protected from the sun’s heat by expansive tree canopies whose branches seem to hold hands in cooperation, not one willing to overgrow or push into another. Pollinators buzz about the native Mountain Laurels, one of the world’s most unique blossoms. The gentlest touch sends blasts of pollen showers over a bee’s body. Your attention quickly diverts to a butterfly, haphazardly fluttering on the way into the safety of their home, high above.
Keep walking, there’s more wonder inside.

The forest understory. Credit: Sierra Farris

You come across a vernal pool. Easily overlooked, these biodiverse hotspots are small but mighty in ecological importance. These are nature’s little nursery for frogs, salamanders and essential insects which call these pools home. These are places where chemical intrusion can spell ecological disaster on a major scale, now and years to come.
Stop and listen. It’s so quiet, you can hear a nearby stream trickling toward the river. And there’s even more. Keep going deeper into the forest.
Underfoot, a thousand miles of mycorrhizae, aka wood-wide-web, transports nutrients, moves water, and feeds all life through an extensive, highly connected subterranean system. This all-important hidden and delicate infrastructure helps the forest adapt to climate change, nourishes tree saplings growing under a closed canopy and serves as a 24-hour banking system that barters for carbon, phosphorus, and nitrogen to feed plants in need. Mycorrhizal networks take decades to establish, yet are obliterated in mere seconds by heavy logging machinery. Their loss spells disaster for life all around.
Though our eyes can see so much wonder, there are species, seemingly invisible, not by magic, but by forest design — bats, owls, bobcats, coyotes down to the tiniest microbiota — that keep the forest ecosystem in balance, unbeknownst to the human recreator. Without them, no such balance can occur and no amount of forest management can replicate their habitat, custom made by nature. Road building and logging not only introduce invasive species but also sever contiguous migratory corridors, making urban-wild boundaries ripe for surprise encounters.
Your mind and body refreshed, the journey ends where it started. We climb into our cars, shaded by the elders towering above. Though absent of words, the forest is grateful to live on another day, sustaining innumerable species that depend on each other for survival. The Preserve also nourishes the human visitor, providing an outdoor classroom of enrichment for young, developing minds and bodies — a rare and invaluable counterbalance in a world where screens compete for every waking moment.
Logging the Preserve threatens one of a few remaining mature coastal forests — one that took shape long before our ancestors arrived. Left intact, the forest will continue to consume large amounts of carbon from our warming atmosphere. Logging causes extensive soil damage, leaving behind hot, arid conditions that many plant and microbial species cannot survive. Roads seed invasive species, often controlled with chemicals that cause unintended damage to native habitat close-by and downstream.
 Our state flower, the Mountain Laurel, is targeted for thinning or removal as are large stands of oak, our state tree. Nature, left alone, has self-managed and adapted over eons, without intrusion of chainsaws and roads. With nature as her witness, the forest knows what we are only beginning to understand how to adapt and survive on a warming planet. If only we would stop and listen.
This is your moment to act. There is a hearing Wednesday, September 16, 2026 at 9 a.m. Old Saybrook Town Hall. Show up. Speak up. The trees, the wildlife, and the generations who come after us are counting on it.
Sierra Farris lives in Essex.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Opponents of new abortion law eye 2028 repeal effort
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: A new coalition filed paperwork seeking to suspend and ultimately repeal the measure in the 2028 election cycle.
text:
ACTIVISTS ANGERED OVER a new law that removes barriers to abortions later in pregnancy have filed paperwork seeking to suspend and ultimately repeal the measure in the 2028 election cycle.
The Compassionate Care Coalition launched this week and filed initial paperwork with Secretary of State Bill Galvin’s office Tuesday to try to topple the law that removed four criteria from statute that enabled abortions after 24 weeks’ gestation, specifically in life-threatening situations. The law instead gives deference to providers’ medical judgment.
Massachusetts Citizens for Life and Massachusetts Family Action are spearheading the effort to repeal the law (H 5595/Chapter 188) that Gov. Maura Healey signed on August 10, said coalition chair Sam Miele.
“Obviously, you know, we’re not trying to outlaw abortion or anything,” Miele told the News Service Friday. “We simply believe that what the law that Maura Healey just passed is not compassionate. It’s not safe for women. It’s very dangerous, actually, for women’s health. And we believe that what was instituted prior was enough.”
Reproductive care advocates say doctors previously felt hamstrung by the four criteria in state statute, and that the new law will ensure pregnant individuals facing serious complications will no longer need to travel out of state to seek care.
The legislation unexpectedly advanced at the end of formal sessions in July. The House passed the bill on a 119-33 vote on July 22, while the Senate passed it on a voice vote on July 31 without placing individual senators on the record. The bill was co-sponsored by Rep. Christine Barber, who lost her Senate primary bid Tuesday to Rep. Erika Uyterhoeven.
“Abortion is on the ballot this November in Massachusetts and around the country,” Healey told reporters after she signed the law. “My opponents are anti-abortion. One of my opponents, Mike Minogue, is proudly anti-abortion.”
The new repeal effort could elevate the topic in this fall’s contest between Healey and Minogue. 
Minogue, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, is openly pro-life due to his Catholic faith. He’s previously said he would “uphold the law” for reproductive rights if he wins the election.
On the day Healey signed the law, Minogue called for an “end to divisive politics.”
“I would much rather see the people of Massachusetts voice their opinion and decide this – not the politicians,” Minogue said last month. “Most people have compassion for women going through such a difficult decision and don’t want this to be a political issue. That said, this is not what I hear voters asking about on the campaign trail.”
Miele said there’s a “very broad” coalition of supporters behind the nascent repeal effort, including pregnancy resource centers and Protestant churches across the state. State public health officials have cracked down on those centers, saying they masquerade as legitimate abortion care providers.
“Before the ink dried on Governor Healey’s politicized signature, we started receiving messages from outraged residents across the state, people sickened that Healey had legalized abortion up to birth for healthy mothers and healthy, pain-capable infants,” Myrna Maloney Flynn, president of Massachusetts Citizens for Life, said in a web post Friday. “Every person who contacted us wanted us to ‘do something’ to restore protections for viable, fully formed babies.”
Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office must now write a summary of the abortion access law, which would be printed on referendum petitions, a Galvin spokesperson said.
Coalition supporters must submit at least 37,289 signatures to local election officials by October 23 to get them certified and make the ballot for 2028, the spokesperson said. Petitions are then due with Galvin’s office on November 6. To suspend the law as the referendum process unfolds, supporters must secure 49,719 signatures.
Healey has the authority to file an emergency preamble to the law to prevent it from being suspended. She flexed that power with the 2024 gun reform law, which is up for a referendum on the November 3 ballot.
A spokesperson for the governor did not directly answer a News Service question about whether Healey would attach an emergency preamble to the abortion access law. 
“This law is for families facing some of the most painful and devastating circumstances imaginable. It’s about parents who were preparing to welcome a baby into their lives and then received a heartbreaking diagnosis late in pregnancy,” Healey said in a statement. “These situations are incredibly rare, and the decisions should be made between patients, their families, and their doctor – not by politicians and the government.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Senator Natalie Murdock discusses energy equity and voting rights
description: As the cost of living continues to soar across the country and worsen the growing divide between the wealthy and everyone else, a major contributor to this troubling trend is the cost of energy and public utilities. Indeed, as North Carolina State Senator Natalie Murdock of Durham and Chatham counties has recently highlighted in […]
text:
Senator Natalie Murdock (Photo: NCGA)  
As the cost of living continues to soar across the country and worsen the growing divide between the wealthy and everyone else, a major contributor to this troubling trend is the cost of energy and public utilities. Indeed, as North Carolina State Senator Natalie Murdock of Durham and Chatham counties has recently highlighted in several forums, the situation has grown so dire that many households one might even think of as middle or working class are finding themselves facing utility shutoffs.
And as Murdock also highlighted, this trend took a deadly and tragic turn recently when a Rocky Mount family that was trying to rely on a generator to provide electricity after having their power shut off, died of carbon monoxide poisoning. And this past week as another climate change-fueled heat wave baked our state, Newsline caught up with the senator for an extended conversation about the tragedy and some of the ways in which our state’s public policies are leaving average residents without basic protections that ought to be basic human rights.
In Part Two of our conversation, we examined another area in which our warming climate is causing suffering – the workplace – as well as two other policy issues that are front and center right now in the public sphere: the growing movement to curb the development of energy-sucking data centers, and the ongoing debate over voting rights and election administration in light of controversial recent actions by North Carolina Republican lawmakers and regulators.
Click here for the full interview with Senator Natalie Murdock.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Political notes: Ivey co-chairs CBCF, Ausby to Appellate Court, another Haley honored
description: Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-4th) co-chairs the annual conference of the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation at a challenging time for the caucus, Simon Haley is honored at UMES and Kendra Young Ausby is elevated to an Appellate Court judgeship, in political notes.
text:
Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-4th)  speaks at an Aug. 25, 2025, rally in Baltimore in support of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, standing behind Ivey, who was wrongly deported to El Salvador earlier in the year. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-4th) will join Rep. Alma Adams (D-N.C.) next week as co-chairs for the  Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s 55th annual legislative conference next week in Washington.
Thousands of elected officials, entrepreneurs and community leaders are expected at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center for the Sept. 16-20 conference, which this year is themed “Rooted, Ready & Rising.” It coincides with the 50th anniversary of the nonprofit caucus foundation that conducts policy research and implements programs. The program will also feature a college fair, a fashion show and about 100 panel discussions on topics such as voting rights, education and criminal justice reform.
“The Annual Legislative Conference has stood the test of time as a homecoming for Black political power and thought,” foundation President and CEO Nicole Austin-Hillery said in a statement. “This year, that has never been more urgent. Rooted, Ready and Rising captures the spirit of a community that has never waited for permission to lead. It is at once a celebration of what has been built over 50 years and a charge to the generation inheriting the work.”
A proud history and a cloudy future: Congressional Black Caucus hit by Supreme Court ruling

Ivey’s turn is the second consecutive year the conference has been co-chaired by a Maryland lawmaker, after Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) served in that position last year. Alsobrooks, who made history in 2024 as the first Black woman from Maryland elected to the U.S. Senate, was part of the largest membership of 62 Democrats in conference history.
Since then, however, the U.S. Supreme Court gutted racial protections in the Voting Rights Act in its April ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, which said states’ use of race-based redistricting is an “unconstitutional racial gerrymander.” Analysts have said the seats of as many as 20 members of the Congressional Black Caucus could be threatened this year, as Republican states have rushed to redraw congressional boundaries less favorable to minority voters.
Ivey was elected in November 2022 and currently serves on the House Appropriations and Ethics committees. Since becoming a member of the caucus, he’s participated in various programs and events and hosted a panel discussion almost three years ago on how a U.S. Supreme Court decision on affirmative action could affect Black-owned businesses.
Another Haley honored at UMES
The University of Maryland Eastern Shore (UMES) on Tuesday will formally rename the university’s School of Agricultural and Natural Sciences in honor of Simon A. Haley, an agriculture educator and the father of Alex Haley, author of the Pulitzer Prize-winning “Roots: The Saga of an American Family.”
Simon Haley was a professor and dean of agriculture. He was born in 1892 and died in 1973. During his life, he served in World War I and the graduated from Agricultural and Technical College State College, now known as North Carolina A&T State University in Greensboro, North Carolina.
When Alex Haley was born in 1921, his father Simon was a graduate student in agriculture at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Alex Haley’s book, “Roots,” which began with stories a young Alex heard family members retell, celebrated its 50th anniversary last month.
According to UMES faculty assembly minutes from February, school officials said that rebranding the agriculture school with Simon Haley’s name “would help distinguish UMES among HBCUs and nationally, as relatively few HBCUs have formally branded schools or colleges.”

The minutes cite Robert Vickers, the school’s vice president for strategic communications and marketing, saying the Haley name “can strengthen institutional visibility, marketing impact, fundraising potential, and alumni engagement, while also enhancing opportunities for partnerships and external support.” They also said the Haley family had been involved in the renaming with Chris Haley, a nephew of Alex Haley’s who works at the Maryland State Archives, acting as family liaison.
Ausby elevated Appellate Court of Maryland
Gov. Wes Moore (D) announced the appointment Thursday of Kendra Young Ausby to a seat on the Appellate Court of Maryland.
Ausby has served as an associate judge on the Baltimore City Circuit since 2010, and was appointed as an associate judge by special appointment on the Appellate Court in 2024. While on the circuit court  bench, she has handled cases ranging from medical malpractice to delinquency to constitutional criminal procedure, according to the governor’s announcement, and has served as the judge in charge of the Family/Domestic Division.
Prior to her time on the bench, she worked as an assistant public defender, an assistant attorney general for the Department of Juvenile Services and principal counsel for the courts and judicial affairs division of the Maryland Office of the Attorney General. Ausby received her law degree from the University of Baltimore School of Law in 1997.
“It is an honor to appoint Judge Kendra Young Ausby to the Appellate Court of Maryland,” Moore said. “With her deep legal expertise and dedication to her community, I know Judge Ausby will advance justice under the law and serve our state well.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Citizenship should not come with an asterisk
description: Naturalization is supposed  to be the end of a yearslong journey to becoming an American citizen, writes Richard T. Herman, but in the current climate of immigration enforcement, many foreign-born citizens are wondering how much of a shield it can be.
text:
Citizenship candidates take the oath of allegiance during a naturalization ceremony at the National Archives in  Washington, D.C., in a file photo from 2018. (Photo by Kelsey Bell/National Archives and Records Administration)Lately, I have been receiving phone calls that an immigration lawyer should rarely receive. They are coming from American citizens.
Some naturalized years ago. They have American passports, vote in American elections, work, pay taxes and raise their families here. Yet they are asking questions that reveal how unsettled some naturalized Americans have become: Could the government take away my citizenship? Could I lose my passport? What happens if immigration agents stop me because I look or sound like an immigrant?
Behind those questions is an even more troubling one: If I am an American citizen, why do I still feel as though I have to prove that I belong?
The law provides important reassurance. Citizenship cannot simply be canceled because an administration changes its priorities. Denaturalization requires specific legal grounds and judicial process. But the fact that citizens are asking these questions matters, particularly at a moment when immigration enforcement and citizenship itself are increasingly occupying the same political conversation.
A recent federal court decision in Maryland illustrates the tension. On Aug. 3, U.S. District Judge Adam Abelson blocked a USCIS policy that barred nonpartisan nongovernmental organizations from providing voter-registration services at administrative naturalization ceremonies. USCIS has since revised its policy in response to the ruling, once again allowing qualifying organizations to help new citizens register while the litigation continues.
The case is formally about voter registration. Its larger significance is about what happens after someone becomes an American.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Naturalization is supposed to end the immigration journey. After years — sometimes decades — of visas, applications, fingerprints, interviews and government scrutiny, a lawful permanent resident raises a hand, takes the Oath of Allegiance and becomes a citizen. At that moment, the legal line separating that person from other Americans should largely disappear.
Yet other developments are making that line feel less settled. The Justice Department has expanded its pursuit of denaturalization cases, recently describing its own initiative as the nation’s “largest denaturalization effort ever.” Many of those cases involve serious allegations that citizenship was illegally obtained or procured through concealment or misrepresentation. The government has legitimate authority to pursue fraud, with the safeguards the law requires.
But government actions send messages beyond the people named in lawsuits, and some naturalized citizens are hearing a broader one: perhaps citizenship is not quite as permanent for them as they thought.
Aggressive immigration enforcement adds another layer to that anxiety. ProPublica documented more than 170 instances in which U.S. citizens were held against their will during immigration operations, raids or related encounters during the first nine months of the current administration. That does not mean immigration authorities have the legal power to deport American citizens; they do not. Nor does it establish that every encounter resulted from mistaken citizenship.
For the citizen wondering what happens when an immigration officer approaches him, however, the distinction can feel academic. A passport can prove that you are an American. It cannot guarantee that nobody will first assume otherwise.
After more than three decades practicing immigration law, that is what troubles me most about the calls I am receiving. Some naturalized Americans increasingly seem to believe that citizenship comes with an asterisk, particularly if they were born abroad, speak with an accent or think others perceive them as foreign.
That is not merely an immigration issue. It is an American one.
There is a profound difference between telling someone that she is a citizen and building a society in which she confidently knows that she will be treated as one. Naturalization is supposed to transform “them” into “us.” If citizens continue to feel that they must carry documents to demonstrate their Americanness, or worry that the immigration system they supposedly left behind can suddenly reach them again, that transformation is incomplete.
The Maryland case offers a timely reminder of what naturalization is supposed to mean. A person enters the ceremony as an immigrant and leaves it as a citizen, entitled to participate fully in American civic life.
There should not be one category of Americans presumed to belong and another expected to prove it.
Citizenship is supposed to settle the question of belonging. When the Oath of Allegiance ends, the immigrant has become an American.
There should be no asterisk after that sentence.

Patricia Stottlemyer (Courtesy photo) 
Each year around the Labor Day holiday, the international nonprofit, Oxfam, conducts and releases a study in which it ranks the best and worst states in the U.S. to work. The researchers preparing the report examine a long list of indicators – more than three dozen – that help them determine how well average workers are paid, treated, and respected in the workplace in hopes of inspiring public officials to enact more and better worker-friendly laws and policies.
Unfortunately, for North Carolina workers, the 2026 Best States to Work Index once again confirms what so many of them already know: namely, that our state does a lousy job in this area. Indeed, as Newsline learned this past week in a conversation with Oxfam America’s labor rights policy lead Patricia Stottlemyer, at a time in which the national affordability crisis is making life harder and harder for average households, the new index ranks our state dead last in the nation.

title: Smyrna High School Football Starts the 2026 Season with Win over Red Lion
description: The Smyrna Eagles (1-0) defeated Red Lion Christian Academy (0-1), 38-0, on September 4, during the first week of Delaware high school football competition.   BEAR, DE — Smyrna quarterback Drew Marks stood in the shotgun formation with his feet at the Red Lion 40 yard line, sophomore running back Terrell Ingram to his right, three receivers lined up to ... R[...]
text:
This image was generated using AI.
The Smyrna Eagles (1-0) defeated Red Lion Christian Academy (0-1), 38-0, on September 4, during the first week of Delaware high school football competition.
 
BEAR, DE — Smyrna quarterback Drew Marks stood in the shotgun formation with his feet at the Red Lion 40 yard line, sophomore running back Terrell Ingram to his right, three receivers lined up to the left and a lone receiver on the right. Marks caught the snap and surveyed the field, but was unable to find an open receiver from the pocket. The senior signal caller rolled to his left looking for a throwing lane and found a small window to deliver the ball to junior receiver Mikiah Jackson.
Jackson was the lone receiver on the right and streaked toward the left sideline during his route. As Marks rolled to his left, Jackson turned his route upfield and Marks lofted a pass toward Jackson’s back shoulder. Jackson made the initial catch as he spun around contorting his body to make the grab, but as he did, the ball came loose and got tipped in the air. Jackson fell to the ground as the ball descended, but Jackson quickly refocused and lunged from the ground to complete the catch before the ball hit the grass. 
Jackson’s highlight catch put the Eagles in the red zone and in position for their fourth score of the first half.
“I just saw it and I knew I could make some way to catch it and I caught it,” Jackson said postgame.
Jackson finished the game with over 100 yards receiving and three receiving touchdowns in Smyrna’s, 38-0, victory over Red Lion, Friday night, ushering in a new season of Delaware high school football.
“It feels amazing to play against another jersey,” Smyrna sophomore Amari Ashley said postgame. “It feels good to go out there and show everybody what we can do.” 
The Eagles played well on both sides of the ball, scoring on all four of its first half offensive drives getting production through the air and on the ground. 
The Eagles first touchdown came on their opening drive in which they traversed 70 yards downfield in 13 plays. The drive was capped off by a four yard touchdown run from senior Chrystian Carroll. Smyrna’s second touchdown was scored by Jackson on a 50-yard catch and run at the end of the first quarter.
Jackson scored his second touchdown of the first half on Smyrna’s subsequent drive, before making the tip catch on the Eagles’ fourth drive which ended in a one yard touchdown run from Ingram.  
“We’re just gonna go at you every play,” Jackson said about what makes Smyrna’s offense dynamic. “I mean, [it’s] a tempo offense, so we don’t let up our foot on the gas and we just go at you every play and drill it down.”
Smyrna’s fourth scoring drive was set up by an interception from sophomore Amari Ashley as Red Lion threatened in Smyrna territory. Ashley’s interception was the first of two interceptions for the Eagles throughout the game and was a part of a strong defensive showing for the program. 
“I saw the quarterback drop back and then I saw them do the post-wheel that we study everyday,” Ashley said describing his interception. “So, I just did everything we did in practice and went up and got it. Just trying to be an athlete.”
Smyrna’s defense never allowed Red Lion to generate any offensive momentum and when the Lions made it into Smyrna territory, the Eagles were able to stop them before they reached the endzone.   
Red Lion found some offensive success through the air with key throws from freshman quarterback Chase Manlove and strong runs by senior Jordon Jones, but the Lions were unable to string those plays together and breakthrough against Smyrna’s defense. 
Red Lion will have a week off before they play again on Saturday, September 19, against Long Island Lutheran High School from New York. That game will be played in Bear at 1:00 p.m. and will be the first out of state test for last season’s Class 2A champion.
Smyrna’s next game will be a road game against Frederick High School on Thursday, September 10, in Frederick, Maryland. This game will be the first of two out of state opponents Smyrna faces before the program takes on its first Class 3A opponent in Middletown on October 2.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Labor votes: Discontent will accompany blue‑collar voters to the polls in the midterm
description: When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?” All workers – unionized or not – are dealing with higher prices for food and gasoline. For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is […]
text:
President Donald Trump greets a retired UAW autoworker while speaking at the General Motors Milford Proving Ground on July 27, 2026, in Milford, Mich. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?”
All workers – unionized or not – are dealing with higher prices for food and gasoline.
For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is bleak. Threats from AI and robotics abound. Pledges by U.S. and international corporations to invest in new plants remain largely pledges. The roughly 400,000 federal job cuts during President Donald Trump’s second term have disrupted lives. Many of these jobs were previously represented by labor unions.
As a labor studies scholar, I believe weariness and wariness will accompany blue-collar voters to the polls in November. As such, the candidates who have practical ideas for turning the economy around and exhibit empathy for Americans worried about how to pay their bills could receive the bulk of the union vote.
The union vote
Over generations, the majority of union members have sided with Democratic candidates, even if that support has wavered since the 1970s.
The 2024 presidential campaign was no exception. The majority of union members voted for Democratic candidates, but at a far lower rate than in the 1960s.
Why does this matter in 2026?
Union voters play a bigger role in Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Nevada, three swing states where the share of voters who belong to unions is above the national average of 10%. In closely contested House and Senate races, even a small shift in union votes could influence the outcome.
What’s in store this November?
How large is the union vote?
The latest Bureau of Labor Statistics figures show that the percentage of U.S. unionized workers has fallen over the past four decades.
In 1983, 20.1% of U.S. workers were represented by a union. In 2025, the rate was 10.0%, or 14.7 million people. Union membership among public sector workers (32.9%) is more than five times higher than that of private sector workers (5.9%). In close elections, the volatility of these voting blocs matters.
During the 2024 presidential campaign, Trump promised to reduce consumer prices, bring back manufacturing jobs and respect workers’ rights.
As the midterm elections approach, I believe the president’s performance on these issues in the eyes of union voters will determine which party controls the House and Senate. And the signs are not promising for Trump, with recent polls indicating the president’s support among union households is eroding.
Manufacturing jobs and inflation 
The U.S. economy has lost 75,000 manufacturing jobs since January 2025, a 0.6% decline. These jobs have steadily declined since the 1980s, so Trump’s policies are not solely to blame.
Furthermore, Trump’s off-again, on-again tariffs may help some U.S. manufacturers. That’s because tariffs can erase the advantages of low-cost overseas labor. As economist Laura Veldkamp noted in July 2026, Trump’s tariffs “made it more profitable for American manufacturers to set up and produce here.”
The bigger problem, though, is that even if some manufacturing returns to the U.S., the work will likely be done with the latest manufacturing technologies, which tend to reduce the need for workers. That does not bode well for significant job creation.
In July 2026, Moody’s financial analyst Mark Zandi told Marketplace that more manufacturing output “doesn’t translate into jobs.” He explained that there has been more activity in the tech sector and in the defense-aerospace industries, but “these factories just don’t employ a lot of people.”
Additionally, Trump has not established a clear plan to lower inflation. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reports that food prices in July 2026 were up 3.0% from July 2025. This increase is slightly above the historical average.
There’s one more factor to consider. Many older blue-collar workers — many of them former union members — across New England, the Great Lakes, Ohio, and western Pennsylvania remain angry about the epic industrial collapse of the 1970s and 1980s.
This kind of generational suffering can show up in the voting booth in a big way. And I don’t think voter surveys and polls are able to measure the depths of this rage.
Union representation
The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 allowed government workers to unionize. But a March 2025 White House announcement said the legislation had enabled “hostile Federal unions to obstruct agency management.”
Through an executive order and mass layoffs across the federal workforce in 2025, Trump has presided over a dramatic change in public sector collective bargaining in Washington, D.C.
Offering guidance on the 2025 executive order, the U.S. Office of Personnel Management directed federal agencies to end their collective bargaining agreement.
In response, the American Federation of Government Employees condemned the action in an email to its members, saying the Trump administration was “illegally strip(ping) collective bargaining rights from hundreds of thousands of federal workers.”
Federal unions have challenged the White House’s March 2025 executive order. In 2026, independent arbitrators have also ruled against the administration’s efforts to circumvent labor agreements with some federal workers. And in June 2026, a federal judge in Massachusetts struck down an effort by the Trump administration to exercise control over union elections at federal agencies.
Whether unionized industrial workers support their public sector counterparts remains to be seen.
Robert Forrant is a professor in the History Department at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, teaching courses on global labor issues, labor history, immigration, and international development. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Montgomery Council member Jawando recovering from heart attack
description: Montgomery County Councilmember Will Jawando, the Democratic nominee for county executive, is recovering from a heart attack that he suffered during a basketball game over the weekend, his office reported Monday.
text:
Montgomery County Councilmember Will Jawando at a June 1 event in Silver Spring for his county executive bid. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Montgomery County Councilmember Will Jawando, the Democratic nominee for county executive, is recovering from a heart attack that he suffered during a basketball game over the weekend, his office reported Monday.
According to the statement, Jawando was playing a regular weekend pickup basketball game on Saturday morning when he experienced the heart attack. He was taken to George Washington University Hospital, “where doctors successfully placed a stent. His doctors are confident in his full recovery given his strong overall health.”
Jawando was reported to be resting comfortably at the hospital Monday, with doctors expected to discharge him later this week to recover at home. Jawando has been directed by his doctor to adjust his office activities in the coming weeks to allow for his recuperation, but his office will remain open to deal with constituent needs, the statement said.
“Councilmember Jawando and his family are grateful to God for the friends who acted quickly and to the exceptional doctors, nurses, and staff at The George Washington University Hospital. They are deeply thankful for the outpouring of support and prayers from neighbors, colleagues, and supporters from across the county and state,” the statement said.
Jawando, a native of Silver Spring, was first elected to an at-large seat on the county council in 2018 and reelected in 2022. He dropped a 2024 bid for U.S. Senate that was won by Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.). He ran for county executive this year, winning 40% of the Democratic primary vote in June to beat fellow council members Andrew Friedson (1st District) who took 34% of the vote and Evan Glass (At-large) who finished with 22% of the primary vote.
He faces Republican Esther Wells in the Nov. 3 general election, when Jawando is favored in the heavily Democratic county.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Angela Freeman case highlights changes in missing person investigations
authors: Morgan Gill, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center and Jayla Jones, RHCJC
description:
A missing-person profile for Angela Freeman includes a photograph taken before she disappeared
and information about her last known sighting in Petal, Mississippi, in September 1993.
text:
PETAL — More than three decades after 17-year-old Angela Freeman disappeared in Petal, a new Mississippi law is changing how law enforcement agencies respond when someone is reported missing. 
The law, passed as House Bill 377 and effective July 1, prohibits law enforcement agencies from requiring a waiting period before accepting a credible missing person report. It also establishes requirements for investigating missing and unidentified people. 
Freeman was last seen at a Pizza Hut in Petal on Sept. 10, 1993. Her case remains unsolved as the 33rd anniversary of her disappearance approaches, illustrating the challenges investigators face as a disappearance stretches from an initial search into a decades-old cold case.
When someone goes missing 
The Forrest County Sheriff’s Office begins investigating as soon as it receives a missing person report, according to Jamie Humphrey, major of operations at the sheriff’s office. 
“There’s a bad misconception that people have now, especially with the new law, that you must wait so many hours to report someone missing,” he said. 
The law also prohibits agencies from requiring a missing person’s next of kin to appear in person before an investigation can begin. 
Deputies are dispatched to where the person was last seen and begin determining what may have happened. Humphrey said the circumstances could include a runaway, missed curfew, kidnapping, medical emergency or possible foul play. 
Federal law requires law enforcement agencies to enter information about certain missing young people into the FBI’s National Crime Information Center within two hours of receiving a report. Humphrey said the quicker it’s input, the faster that information is available to other law enforcement agencies. 
How the search unfolds
Rusty Keyes speaks during an interview about the investigation of missing-person cases. Keyes said the emotional toll can linger for officers, particularly when they are unable to bring someone home.  Credit: RHCJC News
Investigators look at who is missing, when the person was last seen and what may have led to the disappearance. 
“You’ve got to ascertain first what the facts and circumstances centered around that person initially,” said Rusty Keyes, assistant vice president of public safety and chief of police at the University of Southern Mississippi. 
Investigators may develop what law enforcement calls a victimology, examining the person’s habits, relationships, frequently visited places and other details that could provide clues. 
A physical search can expand beyond law enforcement to include firefighters, emergency medical personnel, volunteers, family members and community organizations. Teams may use drones, horses, four-wheelers, aircraft and infrared technology. 
The search for answers can continue after an active search ends. Meaghan Good, founder and administrator of the Charley Project, maintains a public database of cold missing person cases that can include details not found on traditional missing person flyers, such as identifying tattoos. 
Good said keeping publicly accessible information can generate attention and potential leads years after a disappearance. 
“If the missing person’s case isn’t in the database to begin with, then no one knows how to look,” Good said. 
When a case goes cold 
As time passes without answers, investigators face new obstacles. Witnesses become difficult to locate and memories fade. 
“The older the case is, obviously, you get into situations where witnesses or suspects have died,” Humphrey said. 
Humphrey began working on Freeman’s case in 2016 as part of a cold case unit, reviewing previous investigative work and reinterviewing people connected to her disappearance. 
That review help investigators uncover new information and prompted new questions previous investigators had not asked, Humphrey said. Multiple agencies have worked on Freeman’s case, and leads continue to be reviewed. 
“I can’t tell you how many hundreds of people have been interviewed just from us,” Humphrey said. 
Technology can give investigators options that were unavailable when Freeman disappeared. Keyes said investigative genetic genealogy can help in some cold cases when suitable DNA evidence is available, but Humphrey said newer technology does not replace traditional investigative work. 
“Use the old stuff, the old ways. That still works,” Humphrey said. 
Freeman’s family will mark 33 years since her disappearance with a remembrance ceremony at 6 p.m. Sept. 12 at Hinton Park in Petal. 
For investigators and families, an unsolved disappearance can have an impact long after the initial search ends. 
“There’s cases that stand out in me that hurt,” Keyes said. “Maybe I didn’t get to bring someone home.” 
“When someone has been missing for like decades, the wound never closes,” Good said. “These people, they will be afflicted by this for the rest of their lives until the case is solved and perhaps even afterwards.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Labor votes: Discontent will accompany blue‑collar voters to the polls in the midterms
description: When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?” All workers – unionized or not – are dealing with higher prices for food and gasoline. For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is […]
text:
Susan J. Demas
When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?”
All workers – unionized or not – are dealing with higher prices for food and gasoline.
For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is bleak. Threats from AI and robotics abound. Pledges by U.S. and international corporations to invest in new plants remain largely pledges. The roughly 400,000 federal job cuts during President Donald Trump’s second term have disrupted lives. Many of these jobs were previously represented by labor unions.
As a labor studies scholar, I believe weariness and wariness will accompany blue-collar voters to the polls in November. As such, the candidates who have practical ideas for turning the economy around and exhibit empathy for Americans worried about how to pay their bills could receive the bulk of the union vote.
 The union vote

Over generations, the majority of union members have sided with Democratic candidates, even if that support has wavered since the 1970s.
The 2024 presidential campaign was no exception. The majority of union members voted for Democratic candidates, but at a far lower rate than in the 1960s.
Why does this matter in 2026?
Union voters play a bigger role in Michigan, Pennsylvania and Nevada, three swing states where the share of voters who belong to unions is above the national average of 10%. In closely contested House and Senate races, even a small shift in union votes could influence the outcome.
 What’s in store this November?

How large is the union vote?
The latest Bureau of Labor Statistics figures show that the percentage of U.S. unionized workers has fallen over the past four decades.
In 1983, 20.1% of U.S. workers were represented by a union. In 2025, the rate was 10.0%, or 14.7 million people. Union membership among public sector workers (32.9%) is more than five times higher than that of private sector workers (5.9%). In close elections, the volatility of these voting blocs matters.
During the 2024 presidential campaign, Trump promised to reduce consumer prices, bring back manufacturing jobs and respect workers’ rights.
As the midterm elections approach, I believe the president’s performance on these issues in the eyes of union voters will determine which party controls the House and Senate. And the signs are not promising for Trump, with recent polls indicating the president’s support among union households is eroding.
 Manufacturing jobs and inflation

The U.S. economy has lost 75,000 manufacturing jobs since January 2025, a 0.6% decline. These jobs have steadily declined since the 1980s, so Trump’s policies are not solely to blame.
Furthermore, Trump’s off-again, on-again tariffs may help some U.S. manufacturers. That’s because tariffs can erase the advantages of low-cost overseas labor. As economist Laura Veldkamp noted in July 2026, Trump’s tariffs “made it more profitable for American manufacturers to set up and produce here.”
The bigger problem, though, is that even if some manufacturing returns to the U.S., the work will likely be done with the latest manufacturing technologies, which tend to reduce the need for workers. That does not bode well for significant job creation.
In July 2026, Moody’s financial analyst Mark Zandi told Marketplace that more manufacturing output “doesn’t translate into jobs.” He explained that there has been more activity in the tech sector and in the defense-aerospace industries, but “these factories just don’t employ a lot of people.”
Additionally, Trump has not established a clear plan to lower inflation. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reports that food prices in July 2026 were up 3.0% from July 2025. This increase is slightly above the historical average.
There’s one more factor to consider. Many older blue-collar workers – many of them former union members – across New England, the Great Lakes, Ohio and western Pennsylvania remain angry about the epic industrial collapse of the 1970s and 1980s.
This kind of generational suffering can show up in the voting booth in a big way. And I don’t think voter surveys and polls are able to measure the depths of this rage.
 Union representation

The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 allowed government workers to unionize. But a March 2025 White House announcement said the legislation had enabled “hostile Federal unions to obstruct agency management.”
Through an executive order and mass layoffs across the federal workforce in 2025, Trump has presided over a dramatic change in public sector collective bargaining in Washington, D.C.
Offering guidance on the 2025 executive order, the U.S. Office of Personnel Management directed federal agencies to end their collective bargaining agreement.
In response, the American Federation of Government Employees condemned the action in an email to its members, saying the Trump administration was “illegally strip(ping) collective bargaining rights from hundreds of thousands of federal workers.”
Federal unions have challenged the White House’s March 2025 executive order. In 2026, independent arbitrators have also ruled against the administration’s efforts to circumvent labor agreements with some federal workers. And in June 2026, a federal judge in Massachusetts struck down an effort by the Trump administration to exercise control over union elections at federal agencies.
Whether unionized industrial workers support their public sector counterparts remains to be seen.
Robert Forrant, Professor of U.S. History and Labor Studies, UMass Lowell

name: Michigan Advance
title: This Labor Day and beyond, Michigan’s workers demand power, respect
description: For most of my early life, Labor Day was an appreciated holiday, but not the most remarkable one. On the scale of holidays — and I think I speak for most average Americans here — Labor Day ranked toward the bottom compared to the Big Three: Christmas, Halloween, and Thanksgiving. When you have the boundless […]
text:
Pro-labor activists at a climate protest before the 2019 Democratic debate in Detroit. | Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan AdvanceFor most of my early life, Labor Day was an appreciated holiday, but not the most remarkable one. On the scale of holidays — and I think I speak for most average Americans here — Labor Day ranked toward the bottom compared to the Big Three: Christmas, Halloween, and Thanksgiving.
When you have the boundless energy of youth and a full social calendar, Labor Day for me was that last chance to take a dip in the pool with friends before the October chill and enjoy that last barbecue of the season. The “Labor” part of Labor Day? Never really gave it much thought.
But as I got into my 30s, life happened, or rather death happened, to be more precise. When death happens, you start to look at everything that happens in life after that through a different lens. For me that was the death of my mother, Sandy, who passed away just over a decade ago two months after her 65th birthday. The retirement she had spent years dreaming about — a trip to France, buying her first Buick, and hours spent with grandkids — all washed away with memory in its place.
The only thing Sandy did better than working was motherhood. She was such a hard worker that when she passed, the managing editor at the local newspaper, where she devoted untold hours as the office worker equivalent of a multipurpose, multitasking Swiss Army knife, wrote a column about her in tribute. Later she would even work through the cancer treatments before the sarcoma took her after two hard years of chemo and a brief course of radiation.
Today, Labor Day has taken on a whole new meaning for me, and I don’t think I’m alone in that. As the summer of 2026 comes to a close with the midterm elections coming fast, I think Labor Day has become different for a whole lot of working people who are in the struggle, caring for kids and family amidst a broken system that works for the wealthy privileged few, and not for the many.
We are starting to awaken to the power and meaning of the valuable labor we provide — those irreplaceable hours spent in productivity that make this beautiful country run, and all the decades past where we haven’t gotten our fair share of the gains.
This Labor Day, working families are saying enough is enough. We’re fed up with a system that only works for the billionaires, where honest work is not compensated adequately, politicians disrespect their constituents at every vote, and money in politics has made our say in the political process less powerful.
Nothing exemplifies that better than the “Big Beautiful Bill” from last summer. That piece of legislation further broke a health system that helps millions just to reward billionaires with lavish tax cuts. Imagine the world we could live in if Congress prioritized everyday Americans with the same care? What world could we build together if our needs for quality and affordable care were met? If we made enough money to save for retirement, or if prices were manageable and not making most Americans choose rent or groceries just to get by?
Today society is driven by broken incentives and terribly misguided priorities, and I speak to that both as a caregiver and as a healthcare worker at Michigan Medicine.
The week before my mother died, I married the best man on Earth who also happens to have an older brother with Parkinson’s disease. Diagnosed at 30, Parkinson’s took everything from him — the opportunity for a career, to accrue savings, and to live an independent life. We are his caregivers. Because we live in a political system that prioritizes health insurance profit margins and politics over people, cuts to Medicaid and the affordability crisis have meant that he has to live in an adult foster care facility that is nearly an hour away from the rural area where me and my husband live.
Various UA union pins on display at the labor organization’s training facility located in Lansing, Mich. April 6, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
We can’t afford a caregiver for him out of pocket, so we must rely on Medicaid. Those invaluable yet somehow underpaid home health aides that could care for him at home are priced out of the housing market here where we live. Like I said: broken incentives and misguided priorities everywhere you look. We can do better, and we must.
With the Midterms around the corner, working families like mine demand better and we demand it now. We demand the things that will help us not just survive, but thrive, starting with money, power, and respect. Our wallets are empty, especially the sandwich generation, who care for our elders while also supporting kids and other family. We demand change.
We need Ppower at our jobs, which my union contract affords me, but also power to shape our government for workers, not billionaires. This November, working people will exercise the power we have in numbers to fire politicians who coddle the ultra-rich and elect candidates who will work toward a future for all.
Finally, we demand respect. We demand basic human dignity: dignity that is more important than corporate profits, billionaires’ greed, and AI data center techno-feudalism that threatens our health, our jobs, and our property rights.
So to the working people like myself out there: I hope you get that last chance of 2026 to enjoy that barbecue or last day at the pool or a picnic or whatever your plans are: you’ve earned all that and more. But remember that Labor Day is about more than that. Let this Labor Day also be the day where working people say enough is enough and we will show it at the ballot box.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Football weekend that was: Ole Miss survives while State, USM and JSU romp
description: Mississippi kicker Lucas Carneiro (17) celebrates kicking the game-winning field goal during the second half of an NCAA college football game against Louisville, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn.
text:
Let’s look back at Mississippi’s first big college football weekend. And let’s start with No. 9 Ole Miss, which survived No. 24 Louisville, 41-38, in a thriller that began with a first half defensive struggle that turned into a second half shootout.
Rick Cleveland
“Hotty Toddy” is the usual Ole Miss refrain after a hard-fought victory, especially a nationally televised win over a really good team. But that wasn’t the case Sunday night in Nashville when the most audible Rebel reaction was a collective, “Whew!”
“Whew” because Ole Miss survived a two-turnover deficit, first half offensive stumbles, a second half defensive collapse, several crucial injuries and what coach Pete Golding correctly called “a really good Louisville team.” Golding was also dead-on when he told the post-game interviewer, “We got a lot of work to do.”
Better to do that extensive work with a 1-0 record than with the alternative that suddenly became quite likely when Louisville erased a 38-24 lead in a four-minute span late in the fourth quarter. Bottom line: Trinidad Chambliss, the Rebels’ fearless quarterback, wasn’t going to let the Rebels lose. He threw for 336 yards and three touchdowns and ran for 50 yards and another touchdown. 
And, when it mattered most after Louisville tied the game with a minute, 28 seconds remaining, Chambliss led the Rebels 40 yards against the clock to set up Lucas Carneiro’s 48-yard, game-winning field goal as time expired.
Facing third and six at his own 40 with 42 seconds remaining, Chambliss cooly hit tight end Caleb Odom with an 18-yard dart over the middle to extend the drive. Odom, who began his college career at Alabama, also caught a touchdown, while Deuce Alexander, a rocket of a wide receiver, caught two touchdowns.
Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) looks to throw a pass during the first half of an NCAA college football game against Louisville, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn.  Credit: AP Photo/George Walker IV
Most concerning for Golding has to be the injuries to key players, such as preseason All American running back Kewan Lacy, who missed nearly all the second half with what appeared to be a leg bruise. The Rebels also lost defensive lineman Kam Franklin, who was a force before leaving the game, linebacker Keaton Thomas, guard Delano Townsend and offensive tackle Tommy Kinsler. The nature and extent of their injuries are not known. 
The Rebels can probably manage this Saturday’s home opener with Charlotte, a 43-41 loser to The Citadel, without those guys but then comes you-know-who on Sept. 19. One man’s opinion: The LSU team I watched clobber Clemson 51-10 Saturday night would beat the Ole Miss team I watched Sunday night by two touchdowns or more. Yes, much work to do.
Mississippi State 62, UL-Monroe 13
The Bulldogs did what they were supposed to do against an inferior team, putting up other-worldly offensive numbers in the process. State gained 762 yards of total offense, just a smidgeon under a first down per play.
It could have been worse if State coach Jeff Lebby had a sadistic streak. He called off the Dogs early. Kamario Taylor wasn’t as sharp as these eyes have seen him before, so he threw for only 354 yards and four touchdowns without an interception and ran for 59 more and another score. He is going to win some big games for State.
Mississippi State head coach Jeff Lebby calls out to his players during Mississippi State’s NCAA college spring football game, Saturday, April 20, 2024, in Starkville, Miss.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Taylor has more help this season with a deep pool of running backs and receivers and an offensive line that for one night, at least, was dominating. We will see just how much they have improved Saturday. That’s when the Dogs venture into Big Ten country to play at Minnesota, which won seven games and a bowl last year and started the season with a 59-7 crushing of Eastern Illinois.
Both Minnesota and State take a huge step up in competition.
Southern Miss 49, Alcorn State 3
Yes, the Golden Eagles dominated an out-manned team, but they surely looked sharp in doing so. When you consider what little Blake Anderson inherited and the fact that he brought more than 70 new players into the program, his team was crisp and efficient.
“We did what we were supposed to do,” is the way Anderson put it.
Blake Anderson is the University of Southern Mississippi’s new head football coach.
Anderson’s teams usually do. He’s been there before, done this and done it well. He won two Sun Belt championships at Arkansas State. He won one Mountain West championship at Utah State. He had taken nine of the 10 college teams he has coached to bowl games.
Despite missing much of preseason practice with a bruised thumb on his throwing hand, quarterback Ethan Hampton played well after a rusty start. He isn’t the most mobile guy but he has a strong arm and once quarterbacked Northern Illinois to a victory at Notre Dame. So there’s that. A fleet of running backs with varied skills ran well. And the USM defense harassed talented Alcorn quarterback Jaylon Tolbert, intercepting him four times. Kobi Albert, a newcomer at cornerback, swiped three of those.
What Anderson had to say after Saturday night’s win was this: “Now it gets real.”
Yes, it does. Southern Miss will be a decided underdog Saturday at Auburn. 
Jackson State 66, Edward Waters 14
This was the most one-sided matchup of all. Jackson State out-gained the Division II visitors 704-231 and could have scored far more. The question is: Why? Why play this game?
In fact, Edward Waters president A. Zachary Faison Jr. asked himself that same question afterward, and then apologized to players, coaches and fans for allowing the game to be scheduled. You don’t see or hear that every day.
“I owe an apology because the position we placed you in Saturday was not your doing and it was not your coaches’,” Faison wrote in a statement on social media. “The decision was mine.”
Faison indicated he scheduled the game because of a $60,000 guaranty Jackson State paid Edward Waters to make the trip from Jacksonville, Florida. The road trip cost approximately $30,000 in travel expenses, meaning the game netted the Florida school only $30,000.
Faison said a lot more, but I’ll paraphrase. He said Edward Waters will never play a Division I team again. He said 30 grand isn’t nearly a large enough pay day for such a terrible beating.
Jackson State plays host to Tuskegee, another D-II school, albeit a much better football team. Tuskegee defeated Fort Valley State 24-23 last Saturday in Mobile, Alabama.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Decades of August roadside surveys in Iowa show wildlife and habitat changes
description: Every August, for over half a century, Iowa Department of Natural Resource staff have set out along gravel roads at dawn, armed with a set of binoculars and, now, an interactive logging application, to survey the landscape for pheasants and other wildlife.  Todd Bogenschutz, an upland wildlife biologist with DNR, has driven the same 30-mile […]
text:
Young pheasants like to dry off along gravel roads on mornings with heavy dew. Iowa Department of Natural Resources staff use these mornings to count wildlife populations. (Photo courtesy of DNR) Every August, for over half a century, Iowa Department of Natural Resource staff have set out along gravel roads at dawn, armed with a set of binoculars and, now, an interactive logging application, to survey the landscape for pheasants and other wildlife. 
Todd Bogenschutz, an upland wildlife biologist with DNR, has driven the same 30-mile stretch of farm roads in Boone County for the past 30 years. 
On a cloudy, early August morning, he jumped out of his truck, clapping his hands loudly, in an attempt to “flush” a family of pheasants out of the brush they ducked into as the truck inched up.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
With a rustling of feathers, a group of pheasants shot up and rushed to take cover in a nearby cornfield. Bogenschutz used the movement of the birds to count and note the size of the birds to estimate their age.
“Three pigeon-sized birds, no hen,” Bogenschutz said as he stepped back into the truck and grabbed his phone to record the sighting. 
Over the past three decades with DNR, Bogenschutz has seen the landscape — and with it the wildlife — change in tune with weather patterns and federal policies. 
The results from Iowa’s 2026 August roadside survey indicates the second-highest pheasant population Iowa has seen since 2015. Even so, that pheasant population size is less than half of what it was when Bogenschutz started with Iowa DNR in the mid 1990s. The main difference, he said, is habitat availability. 
A large group of pheasants spotted during one of DNR’s August roadside surveys. (Photo courtesy of DNR)
While the 2026 survey showed some of the highest pheasant populations in more than decade, the count was about 17% lower than the count in 2025. 
This year the survey results show an average of 22.6 pheasants per 30-mile route, while last year’s report found an average of 27.5 pheasants per route. Before the turn of the century, averages were commonly above 40 pheasants per route, though in the 2010s, averages dipped below 10 for a stint. 
Bogenshutz said winter precipitation is a good indicator of how big the pheasant population will be, as the birds sometimes have difficulty over-wintering in heavy amounts of snow. Last year, he said, was a mild winter, while this most recent year he considered “average.” 
“A lot of hens die when we have the tougher winters, and so it doesn’t really matter what happens during nesting if we’ve got fewer hens,” Bogenshutz said. “Even if it’s a great nesting year, their count’s probably going down.” 
Cold and wet conditions in the spring, when the birds nest, can also cause a dip in population sizes, but weather reports for spring 2026 showed fairly normal conditions. 
Bogenschutz said based on the weather conditions for the year, staff anticipated no change in pheasant populations from 2025, yet the population decreased “significantly” with decreasing trends in 4 of the 9 survey regions.
Even if a pheasant hen loses her nest, they can often nest a second and sometimes even a third time in a season. Bogenschutz and other DNR staff who conduct the surveys make note of the size of the young birds. If a bird is smaller when staff survey in August, it suggests it came from a second roost, while a pigeon-sized young pheasant indicates a successful first nest. 
Less habitat, fewer birds
While winter weather directly impacts the birds in a season, habitat loss affects bird populations more gradually. 
As Bogenschutz drove along the route, he pointed to fields with rows of corn that he said used to be planted with native grasses, presumably through the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Conservation Reserve Program, or CRP. Along these plots, Bogenschutz said he used to find pheasants or other upland game – but now it’s unlikely they’d be there. 
“If we want to have critters, we’ve got to have habitat, and that’s basically some type of grass,” Bogenschutz said. 
According to the roadside survey report, Iowa has more than 500,000 fewer acres enrolled in CRP than it did in 1995. When looking at total habitat – CRP, hay and small grains habitat – Iowa has lost more than 1.4 million acres of habitat since 1995, according to the survey. 
In his report, Bogenschutz writes that while the 2018 farm bill expanded CRP to 27 million acres nationally, it reduced CRP rental rates which historically tracked closely with agricultural land values. 
Bogenschutz said that since CRP contracts expire after a number of years, if a farmer can get more by planting a cash crop on it – even if the land is subject to flooding or drought – or renting it to another farmer, it’s not uncommon to see the grassland get tilled to make way for corn or soybeans. 
“I think landowners in Iowa generally are willing to be good stewards and they would participate more in CRP,” Bogenschutz said. 
He also sees more strips of CRP or other incentive programs that promote grassland areas. These strips, he said, are good for water quality and allow for some bird habitat, but generally are not as protective as a larger grassed area. When the habitat is just a strip, it leaves nesting birds more vulnerable to attacks from predators. 
While a new farm bill has not materialized in the past several years, current drafts in the House and Senate keep the same 27 million acre cap set in the 2018 law. Several efforts in both chambers were proposed to bolster CRP, however progress on passing a farm bill has stalled as lawmakers disagree over federal nutrition program policies.
Conservation groups like Pheasants Forever also advocate for access to habitat through programs like CRP and by purchasing land that can become permanent habitat and public hunting grounds.
Roadside surveys 
While the landscape around the routes has changed, the routes themselves have been consistent through the years.
The survey started in the 1930s as just a handful of randomly selected, 15-mile routes that staff drove up and back. Now, Bogenschutz said, each county has two, 30-mile routes that stay the same from year to year unless the route gets paved. 
Bogenshutz said testing from Iowa State University in the 1950s “standardized” the roadside survey so that staff would run the routes on mornings with heavy dew and low wind. Those conditions, the study found, were most likely to draw the roosts to the edges of the roadsides as the birds tend to seek dry ground. 
A graph shows Iowa pheasant population changes over the years. (Graph courtesy of DNR)
The survey ultimately helps to inform the DNR about bird populations ahead of the hunting season. 
As Iowa heads into its 101st pheasant hunting season, Bogenschutz’s report said it should be a “good” hunting season as overall pheasant populations are 12% above the 10-year trend. Pheasant counts were above the 10-year averages in all regions of the state, except the south-central region, Bogenschutz reported. 
The report estimates pheasant harvest numbers between 350,000 to 450,000 roosters this fall. Last year, hunters harvested around 500,000 ring-necked pheasant roosters.
DNR staff also survey for other wildlife on the dewy August mornings. According to the report, bobwhite quail populations declined from an average of 1.1 birds per route in 2025, to less than one bird per route in 2026. 
Gray partridge populations appeared to have increased by 6% from 2025 to 2026 and cottontail rabbit populations this year were “identical” to those observed in 2025. No jackrabbits were observed in 2026.
Cottontail rabbit seasons opened at the end of August. Pheasant, gray partridge and bobwhite quail seasons will open at various dates in October. Official dates and hunting information can be found online with DNR.
