name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas students learn about 9/11 attacks through oral histories
description: Army veteran Wesley Jackson remembers his confusion when co-workers told him two planes struck the World Trade Center on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001.  After processing the news of the terrorist attacks, Jackson realized his days as a peacetime soldier were over, and it was only a matter of time before he was deployed […]
text:
Debbie Miller, a journalism instructor at NorthWest Arkansas Community College in Bentonville, discusses a 9/11 assignment with her students on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Army veteran Wesley Jackson remembers his confusion when co-workers told him two planes struck the World Trade Center on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001. 
After processing the news of the terrorist attacks, Jackson realized his days as a peacetime soldier were over, and it was only a matter of time before he was deployed to the Middle East. 
“My whole life changed in an instant,” he said. 
Twenty-five years later, Jackson is teaching Arkansas State University students about the impact of that day as an assistant professor of history. 
Friday marks the anniversary of the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people when hijacked planes crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a rural field in Pennsylvania. Arkansas history, journalism and political science teachers with vivid memories of that day are using oral histories to better explain its significance to students who weren’t alive in 2001. 
Learning history for students isn’t about dates and people, Jackson said.
“It’s the skills they’re learning about — critical thinking, decision making and being good stewards of the future,” he said. 
‘The uncertainty of it all’
Marie Totten, a visiting assistant professor in the University of Central Arkansas’ history department, said her students often hear about 9/11 in the context of conspiracies, and want to learn how to sift through false information. 
“They recognize that they’re addicted to their phones and their phones are created to make them addicted, that the algorithm is created to show them information that may not be true, and they want to learn the skills to combat that,” she said. 
 


Let us know what you think...


 



Some misinformation is dispelled through an oral history assignment that involves Totten’s students interviewing someone, often a grandparent, about their memories of Sept. 11. Talking to a trusted source can help push back against conspiracy theories students see online, she said.
“They’re a very curious generation, they just don’t know who to ask or what questions to ask,” Totten said. 
Jackson said conspiracy websites often use cherrypicked or misleading information, which is why he teaches students the importance of looking at all available evidence. 
Although he can share his personal experiences as a soldier sent to Afghanistan and Iraq because of the Sept. 11 attack, Jackson said like any primary source, he’s just one piece of the puzzle and it’s important to look at multiple sources to see the broader story. 
Jackson also teaches students that the narrative around historical events continuously changes as more information is uncovered. 
TSA shares passengers’ personal information with immigration enforcement, documents show

“That’s why I tell them it’s important to understand that history is an ever-evolving thing,” he said. “It’s a living creature. It’s not set in stone.”
Aneyda Reynaga, a journalism student at NorthWest Arkansas Community College, was born three years after the attacks and said she grew up learning about it at school through sometimes “graphic documentaries” that could make you feel “queasy.”
Education about the attacks typically focuses on the event itself, but it’s also important to discuss what happened after, Reynaga said.
“Growing up, I didn’t even know TSA was because of 9/11, I thought it was always a thing,” she said, referring to the Transportation Security Administration established after the attacks. 
Reynaga recently learned more about the event while interviewing her dad and aunt for a class assignment, and said she was most surprised to hear that their lives went on as usual, with her aunt still expected to go to work that day.  
The assignment also helped Reynaga understand how the attacks affected the entire country. 
“It made me see the uncertainty of it all because Arkansas is so far from New York, and the fact that people felt scared or they felt uncertain of what was going to happen all the way over here, I think it really gave me a new perspective on everything,” she said. 
‘How history transpires’
Debbie Miller, a veteran journalist and instructor at NorthWest Arkansas Community College, said she’s had students like Reynaga write about Sept. 11 over the years, but it felt particularly relevant to discuss this semester in light of the 25th anniversary. 
Interviewing family allows novice journalists, who may prefer communicating via text or email, to have a comfortable space to practice talking and interacting in person, Miller said. The assignment also allows students to connect with family in a way they might not have, she said.
Debbie Miller, a journalism instructor at NorthWest Arkansas Community College in Bentonville, watches as a student shares a video during a 9/11 discussion on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
The attack on Pearl Harbor during World War II was a significant moment for Miller’s parents’ generation, but Miller said she doesn’t recall ever thinking to ask her parents about their experiences. Looking back, Miller said she wishes she had listened more when they were sharing stories. 
“I want to encourage curiosity in a safe space and encourage them to make more connections with their family members that they haven’t really thought about,” she said. 
At John Brown University, political science professor Daniel Bennett has students read a Politico Magazine oral history that describes what it was like aboard Air Force One for the eight hours it was in the air following the attacks. 
Something that resonates with students today is how technologically different the world was 25 years ago, Bennett said. The lack of social media or smart phones and the inability to communicate as easily is “pretty striking for what today’s students are typically familiar with,” he said. 
“We’ll also raise it in the context of how did this affect future conversations about civil liberties in the scope of protecting national security versus individual freedoms, as well as maybe this being the last unifying moment in American politics,” Bennett said. 
For many of today’s students, 9/11 is becoming just another major moment in American history, the same way Pearl Harbor or President John Kennedy’s assassination was remembered by older generations, he said. 
“I think for future generations, it’ll lose the magnitude of how important of a moment it was for myriad reasons,” Bennett said. “I don’t think that’s something to be happy about or even lamentable, it’s just kind of how history transpires.”

title: Concierges, adjuncts, potato chip tasters: US employers relying more on ‘disposable’ workers
description: When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a […]
text:
There’s no way to climb a ladder without rungs.
(Photo: John Lund/Photodisc via Getty Images)
When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a part-timer with no career prospects in that job.
When my best intentions to eat well are for naught and I gorge on Doritos, I remember that the tasters PepsiCo hires to test the chips’ addictiveness are contractors.
These are all examples of what I call “disposable jobs.” People who have them work at an employer’s site, but their employer makes no commitment to them regarding career prospects or job security. My research shows that employers treat more than 1 in 3 U.S. workers as disposable. That comes to just under 57 million full- or part-time workers out of the nation’s workforce of 162 million.
I am a labor economist. In my new book, “Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment,” I explain why this is happening, what forms it takes, how common it is, what the consequences are for people and for society, and what can be done about it.
3 different varieties
To learn more, I commissioned a nationally representative survey of over 6,000 people in late 2022. I also interviewed nearly 100 workers, employers and policymakers.
I found that there are three categories of disposable workers.
1. Contractors who are employed by a staffing firm but work at a client’s site. Examples include temporary office workers, building cleaners and security guards. Many of these people are poorly paid, but some, such as travel nurses, are highly compensated. My survey shows that these contractors account for 13% of the workforce.
2. Freelancers who work for companies, organizations or agencies without being employees. Examples include Uber and Lyft drivers, food delivery drivers, computer programmers and freelance journalists. In my survey, organizational freelancers represent 5% of the workforce. I don’t include in this category freelancers who work for individual people, such as most dog-walkers and handymen, because my focus is on how employers treat their employees.
3. Marginal workers who are employed by companies, organizations or agencies. They lack career opportunities, and their jobs have high turnover built in. Marginal workers account for 17% of the workforce in my survey.
Marginal work is important due to its magnitude and because although those jobs look standard, they are designed to be disposable.
Staff attorneys are quintessential marginal employees. They’re hired by law firms as employees, but the central feature of their jobs is that they are not on the promotion ladder to partner. Unlike their career-track counterparts, they have no job security. They are often hired to do the grunt work on a specific case, with the understanding that there is no commitment to keep them on if business lags or the project ends.
Adjunct professors are another good example. This group includes part-timers who teach a small number of courses and full-time contract faculty, but in both cases they lack job security and aren’t on track to obtain permanent, tenured, academic jobs.
In 1970 people with tenure or tenure-track jobs constituted 73% of those teaching at colleges and universities. By 2021 only 32% had that status, and the rest were adjunct instructors or contract faculty.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Part-time marginal workers
Another example of marginal work is part-timers.
Employing part-time workers costs less than having full-timers on the payroll. Part-time jobs pay an hourly wage that is nearly 20% below what workers with full-time jobs earn after age, education, occupation and industry are taken into account. When benefits are considered, the gap rises by another 5%.
A second advantage of part-timers from the employer’s perspective is higher turnover, which provides an easy path to be able to adjust the size of the workforce and which enables them to avoid investing in career development.
When a team of researchers led by professor Susan Lambert interviewed 88 employers that pay low wages, they found that many use part-time work to make their workforces more “flexible.” One manager explained that high churn of part-timers gave the company so much flexibility that they didn’t need temp workers.
“Temp workers: We don’t need them,” he said. “Wait a day for turnover.”
Evidence that employers try to maximize the number of people working for them part time instead of full time and with benefits arose after the Affordable Care Act fully took effect in 2014.
The ACA requires that employers with 50 or more employees either provide them with health insurance or pay for them to buy it, but only for people who work 30 or more hours a week. Otherwise they pay, as of 2026, a penalty of US$3,340 per uninsured employee.
Another team of researchers compared trends in part-time work in three low-wage industries – retail, hotels and restaurants, before and after the ACA rolled out. They found that the use of part-timers increased by 500,000 in the years after the Affordable Care Act was implemented. This suggests that companies add to their part-time ranks to save on the health insurance costs of standard employment.
Forces behind this trend
Why do employers want many of their workers to be disposable?
A primary motive is to save money. Employing freelancers and contractors means they can avoid mandatory benefits such as Social Security contributions and, for larger employers, contributing to the cost of health insurance.
Marginal workers, to be sure, do receive these benefits. But the high turnover built into their jobs means that their employers can invest less in their training and avoid the management costs otherwise associated with layoff severance and fair treatment on the job.
An additional motive for many employers is a lack of respect for what front-line employees can contribute. A 2023 report from the McKinsey consulting firm illustrated this tendency when it asserted that 5% of employees deliver 95% of “an organization’s value.”
This claim, which I believe is inaccurate, still speaks volumes about the attitude of McKinsey and the firms they interviewed regarding the other 95% of workers. They see those employees as disposable.
Outsourcing cleaning services might seem like a good way to cut costs, but in hospitals it can undercut safety. (Photo: Jupiterimages/BananaStock via Getty Images Plus)
Less pay and job satisfaction
My survey showed that contractors, freelancers who work for employers and marginal employees all earn less than regular workers do.
In addition, the survey found that contractors and marginal workers are notably less satisfied with their jobs compared with regular workers, whereas freelancers, due to their ability to choose where and when to work, are more satisfied.
The public also pays a price for the use of disposable workers. As examples, researchers have found that hospital infection rates rise when cleaners are contract workers and that the use of contractors leads to a higher rate of industrial accidents.
Paul Osterman is professor emeritus at MIT’s Sloan School.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: How many South Carolina college grads stay in state for work?
description: Over the past decade and a half, about 60% of SC college grads went to work in the Palmetto State in the year after receiving their diploma.
text:
Students walk on the grounds of the University of South Carolina campus in Columbia, S.C. , on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA)COLUMBIA — Over the past decade and a half, more than 60% of South Carolina college graduates went to work in the Palmetto State in the year after receiving their diploma.
But by year three, that drops 10 percentage points, and by year five less than half of those same graduates are still working in the state, according to a new study by the state’s employment agency.
On a national basis, South Carolina lands in the middle third of states when it comes to retaining its graduates.
Economists from the state Department of Employment and Workforce tracked technical and four-year college graduates from the class of 2010 through the class of 2023, who are now three years out of school — to see how many stayed in South Carolina to work and how many left to pursue a job or further their education elsewhere.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The study, which relied on unemployment insurance wage records, did not count federal government workers, the self-employed or military members. Researchers also adjusted for students who went on to further their education in South Carolina rather than joining the workforce after graduation.
The study also measured how many students go to work within their field of study.
“Are nursing students becoming nurses or are they working as (medical) office receptionists?” said Erica Von Nessen, one of the researchers.
Lawyers, architects and health care students are the most likely to have careers in South Carolina that most closely match their degrees, the researchers found.
But they also took the data a step further to see how some degree-holders’ skillsets might still translate into jobs not directly related to their studies.
“One of the things we found was there are a substantial number of people with an English major who become paralegals,” researcher Bryan Grady said. “When you think about the skills that you acquire as an English major and the skills that are required to be a paralegal, there’s clearly an overlap there.”
Speaking to manufacturers and business people in Columbia last week at an annual workforce conference put on by the state’s largest industry group, Von Nessen and Grady highlighted findings on some of the state’s most in-demand fields — education, nursing and engineering.
Here’s how many are graduating from SC colleges with in-demand degrees. It’s not enough.

Engineering graduates, for example, tend to take a few years to find work in their field. In the first year after graduation, fewer than 62% of students found work as engineers at South Carolina companies. By year four, that rose to nearly 71%.
Those that didn’t get an engineering job right away still tended to be designers, construction managers, financial analysts or office clerks in the state.
And while the state often talks about struggling to keep teachers in the classroom, Von Nessen said nearly 70% of graduates were still working in education 15 years later.
“That’s very encouraging to me because I was thinking, ‘Oh, are we going to see something like 30% retention,’” she said.
Of nursing graduates, most got jobs in South Carolina right away — 98% — and stayed in them for a long time — 80% remained in the field 15 years later.
On the other hand, Grady said, business graduates were less likely to work in the state. But downtown Charlotte, the country’s second largest banking center, is just 10 miles north of the South Carolina border.
“It doesn’t take a rocket scientist to figure out that they’re going to want some some business majors up there,” he said.
Von Nessen and Grady’s study was part of larger legislative efforts to reshuffle oversight of the state’s workforce development efforts.
A 2023 law put all state-funded workforce development programs under the employment department’s microscope, making sure programs run by various agencies are all delivering on their goals.
Other tenets of the law included an annual analysis of job openings versus college graduates available to fill them.
“I think a lot of the discussion has been around career pathways and pipelines of we just need to plug people into these holes,” Grady said. “But the fact is, there are a lot of factors that determine what kind of job somebody ends up with. How do we make sure that the workforce of South Carolina as a whole has a wide variety of skills that employers are interested in, so that we don’t have to scramble?”
In the future, Von Nessen said they hope to work with colleges to measure how well their efforts to keep graduates in state are working.
More SC colleges want to help pay students who land summer internships

For example, the University of South Carolina offers $3,000 to students who participate in internships in high-demand industries in the state, such as aerospace, automotive, energy, financial services, healthcare, insurance and manufacturing.
More than 2,862 students across the USC college system, 74% of them in-state, have participated. They’ve gone to work for 891 companies across 43 South Carolina counties, according to a statement from the university. The school has awarded more than $8.6 million in stipends since the program started three years ago
Clemson University, too, operates a similar program but the school did not provide updated numbers in time for deadline.
The internship programs are taxpayer funded, with $4 million going to Clemson annually and $3 million now going to the USC system.
Coastal Carolina University had asked state legislators to spend $390,000 annually to start its own Teal Works Program, but the funding didn’t make it into the final budget.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Increasing SNAP error rates could be good news for Florida (really)
description: Florida’s anticipated error rate in the federal food security program called SNAP appears to be on the rise — a move that could wind up helping the state avoid costly penalties in the short run. After dipping to 12.97% for federal fiscal year (FFY) 2025, the unofficial payment error rate for FFY 2026 is an […]
text:
Florida's SNAP error rates are back on the rise. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Florida’s anticipated error rate in the federal food security program called SNAP appears to be on the rise — a move that could wind up helping the state avoid costly penalties in the short run.
After dipping to 12.97% for federal fiscal year (FFY) 2025, the unofficial payment error rate for FFY 2026 is an average 14.49%. (Federal fiscal years open each Oct. 1.)
That’s higher than the anticipated national error rate of 10.62%, also based on data through March, a Department of Children and Families, the Sept. 1, 2026, report shows.
The report does not contain error rates by county. But it does highlight error rates by region.  Northeast Florida had the highest error rates (19.3%), followed by southern Florida (18.81%) and southeast Florida (16.47%).
Payment error rates measure the accuracy of each state’s eligibility and benefit determinations in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. Errors are unintentional mistakes and are not considered fraud.
High error rates don’t bode well for people who rely on the food security program, or for the federal government that until now has footed the entire costs of the program.
But it could be good financial news for Florida, which may avoid having to pay a $1 billion penalty if it wants to continue to participate.  
Enrollment in SNAP has dipped by double digits over the last year — 2,285,099 residents enrolled in the program in June, down from 2,970,283 in June 2025, data maintained by the DCF shows.
That’s about a 23% reduction.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
SNAP provides nutritional support for low-income seniors, people with disabilities living on fixed incomes, and other individuals and families with low incomes. Although funded by the federal government, SNAP in Florida is administered by DCF’s Office of Economic Self-Sufficiency, which is responsible for determining eligibility.
Before the One Big Beautiful Bill Act became law, SNAP benefits were funded entirely by the federal government. The new law slashes $186 billion in funding and for the first time puts cost-sharing requirements on states beginning in FFY 2028.
States with payment error rates of 6% or higher are required to contribute to the costs of food as follows:

5% of the cost of benefits for error rates above 6%.
10% of the cost of benefits for payment rates between 8% and 10%.
15%, of the costs of benefits for error rates above 10%.

On the other hand …
But the federal law delays the cost-sharing requirements for states with comparatively high payment error rates compared to the rest of the nation.
For instance, states with payment errors of 13.33% or more in FFY 2025 aren’t required to contribute to the costs of the program until FFY 2029.
Florida’s payment error rate had been 12.97% and the state didn’t qualify for that one-year delay. Based on the cost-sharing calculations, Florida faced a $1 billion tab beginning Oct. 1, 2027.
However, the law gives states a second chance to delay the cost-sharing requirements by allowing them to use either their FFY 2025 or FFY 2026 error rates.
Florida economists agree that the unofficial  2026 error through March rate is high enough, according to the report, to push cost sharing requirements back another three years.
“If Florida’s final FFY 2026 (payment error rate)  is at least 13.33 percent, implementation of the state cost-sharing requirement would be delayed until FFY 2030,” the Long Term Financial Outlook notes.
Economists annually prepare a  snapshot of the state’s budget situation for the next three years. The outlook, required by the Florida Constitution, is meant to put legislators and other state officials on notice about whether a budget surplus or deficit looms.
